#6864. 6 Antique Trends Designers Are Watching for 2027

Above: The kitchen in designer Phillip Thomas’s Bellport retreat.

Do the words “antique” and “trend” really belong in the same sentence? In many ways, a great antique shop feels like the antidote to trend fatigue: a space where the true must-haves are hidden in dusty corners, with part of the fun in the thrill of the hunt. Yet, as we round out 2026, there’s no denying the current design cycle is casting off perfection for patina. Antiques are en vogue, and top designers are keeping a close eye on the periods, pieces, and yes, trends, that are poised to find new life in 2027.

“The return of interest in antiques reflects a trend towards more personal, unique interiors, and away from strict modern rooms which can often be cool and generic,” says ELLE Decor A-List designer Jamie Drake. This shift paves the way for more playful interactions between pieces, unexpected layering, and unabashed personality.

Other experts second the motion for more character. “I’m seeing clients really drawn to antiques with more to them than meets the eye: pieces that have a bit of humor or whimsy, or pieces with great provenance,” says ELLE Decor Rising Star William Cullum. (He lists a “ridiculously giant butterfly light fixture” from New Orleans, rattan chairs from Bing Crosby’s estate, and a disco ball from Cyndi Lauper’s Bonham’s sale in his list of recent acquisitions—professional and personal.)

Luckily for the amateur antiquer, not all trending vintage styles require a substantial space commitment or glamorous provenance—although an interesting backstory helps. “Antiques are always about a story: where you found them, who owned them, and how that story will continue on after us,” Cullum says.

Ahead, we asked top designers and experts to share the most inspiring antique trends of the moment. From neoclassic mirrors to hand-painted chests paired with modern art, their takes are sure to inform your next estate sale rummage, or inspire you to restyle an old heirloom.

We called mirrored surfaces a major trend to watch for fall 2026, and antique trends have followed suit. Unexpected (or better yet, artfully manipulated) reflections can add rich dimension and movement to any space, but in this category, antiques create a window to the past that’s tough to beat.

“One of the easiest ways to add a sense of history to a room is to include an antique mirror,” says Drake. “Whether you choose a sober and strict neo-classic piece or a more flamboyant baroque one, reflections of the past add depth and sparkle.”

“One trend I’m observing is an uptick in antique dowry chests,” antiques dealer Ali Mahon says. From Pennsylvania Dutch to Swedish Folk and Spanish carved, she’s noticed clients gravitating toward more delicately adorned storage over spare. With thoughtfully mixed furniture (from style to period) becoming more desirable than matching sets, Mahon sees more hand-painted antique surfaces in our future: “With their decorative tulips, leaves, birds, and hearts, dowry chests create a colorful splash in any room.”

ELLE Decor Rising Star Reagan Gail Struble agrees—although delicate designs are not a requirement of the trend, in her book: “Something about a playful wash of color on an awesome old piece of furniture is very alluring, especially when you can see the age and texture of the wood peeking through,” she says. “Hand-painted case pieces add a little punch of charm to any room.”

Luckily, these antiques can be just as functional as they are fashionable. Mahon recommends using a painted chest as a coffee table, at the foot of the bed, or in a space that could benefit from a bit more romance (and a few extra drawers). When styling your find in a modern space, Struble says that contrast is key: try a “chippy Swedish chest of drawers” with an unexpected photograph or painting above it.

According to ELLE Decor A-List designer Nick Olsen, Art Deco pieces are setting the tone for 2027 antique trends—although, if you ask him, they were never out. “I'm particularly inspired by the [art deco influence in the] Gujarat palace in India,” he says. “I'm fascinated by how every element seems to have a wide border: marble floors, carpets, walls of veneer and mohair velvet upholstery.”

According to Olsen, using Art Deco design compositions can do as much for a room as actual pieces from the period. “I like the idea of contrasting borders: solid textures punctuated by smaller graphic prints on furniture and more delicate lighting,” he explains. And while borders are easy to create with paint, paneling, and carpet seaming, Olsen challenges clients to push the Art Deco agenda further by bordering with luxe materials.

Whether you’re new to antiquing or simply trying to add more character to a space, lighting is an excellent place to start. “Lighting is the jewelry of the home, so it’s one of my favorite places to bring in something vintage,” says A-Lister Corey Damen Jenkins. “An Art Deco sconce or an antique brass lantern has a warmth to it that’s hard to find in something brand new.”

Adding to an existing space? Jenkins advises starting small: “Swap one overhead fixture or put a pair of vintage lamps on a console, and you’ll be surprised how much the whole room shifts,” he says. “It’s an easy way to add history without starting over.”

“In light of America’s 250th birthday, Americana in general is in vogue,” says Mahon. Among her clients, the trend has manifested in quilts and textiles, portraits of sea captains, trade signs, and ironstone—culminating in an aesthetic she describes as “elevated country—not corny.”

If you’ve noticed that no particular design period seems to reign supreme among designers’ top antique trend picks, it’s not an accident. Heading into 2027, there’s a strong argument to be made that mixed-period design is more influential than any singular reference.

“I love a room that doesn’t belong to any one decade,” Jenkins says. “A nineteenth-century chest with a 1970s lamp on top, or a Lucite chair pulled up to an antique desk. Those are the pairings that make people stop and look twice.” Drake adds that seemingly out-of-place seating is an easy way to add intrigue. “I love including antique chairs as sculptural notes, contrasted against modern upholstery and tables,” he says.

But when it comes to antiquing, there’s really only so much one can plan for. Letting a great find lead the way often turns out to be a better strategy than arriving to an estate sale with a rigid checklist. The best way to keep up with top designers when it comes to antiquing this year? Find a piece that has something to say, place it where it seems to belong, and then try it where it doesn’t.

#6863. I've Had This Modular Sofa for Four Years, and Its Secret Twin "Bed" Is a Hosting Game-Changer

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The first couch I ordered for my basement was a bust. No matter how hard they tried, the delivery men couldn’t angle it to get it down the narrow stairs. Because I live in a 1930s home, all the charm turns to chaos when it comes to fitting new furniture. I was literally stuck because a family of five was visiting for the holidays and they had nothing to sit (or sleep) on. Plus, what even is a basement without a comfy couch?

Ideally, I wanted a sleeper sofa to accommodate my guests and let my kids have sleepovers. But there was absolutely no way I would risk buying another couch that couldn’t come apart and was stuck in a corner. For round two, I knew that I needed a modular sectional. After a bit of research, I came across the Burrow Range sectional and was elated that it could be assembled like a building-block puzzle that can grow over time if I wanted to add more sections.

Since the basement isn’t huge, my selection was a four-piece model that included two arm pieces as well as an ottoman. Because my dreams of a sleeper were no more, I liked that the Range has flippable top cushions that, when pulled back, could make a twin-size bed. Happily, four years later, the sectional has survived many, many sleepovers and now resides in my bedroom. Read on to see how it transitioned from child-hopping to a peaceful nook two floors up.

Best For: A growing household or someone who likes to change the layout of their space often.

Not ideal for: Someone who is very tall. If you are taller than 6 feet, the sofa may sit too low for you.

Price at review (4-piece sectional lounger): $1,271 (originally $2,119)

Bottom Line: The modular sectional is comfortable and won’t sag or end up with flat cushions, even after years of use.

Because I needed the sectional before the winter holidays, I was glad that I could order by early December and still get my sofa before Santa came to town. The four big boxes for the cushions and a little box for legs came to my front door within a week.

My husband and I brought down all the boxes to the basement where we started to unbox and assemble. The overall process took no more than 30 minutes. In a nutshell, you need to line up the holes with the metal braces and secure those with large plastic knob screws. The cushions have two strips of Velcro that stick to the black fabric at the base to keep them from sliding out from beneath.

The sofa pieces are easy to secure together.

Compared to my living room couch, which is a mid-century modern style West Elm reversible sectional, the Burrow has a bit more bounce to the cushion. While the seats are softer, I would still describe it as medium-firm. As soon as I sit down, it feels relaxing. Because it is only 28 inches high, it is a little lower than I am used to. (This still works out because I can slouch down and stretch my feet up on the ottoman when I watch a movie.)

Later, when I moved the sectional up to my bedroom, I lie across all three seat cushions, with my head resting on the arm cushion, as if I am reading in bed. The arm cushions are slightly angled, with more padding at the bottom to create a gentle incline that supports my head.

I chose the Stone Gray upholstery, an almost salt-and-pepper look, in performance flatweave. This is my third woven upholstery sofa, and it is the softest. It feels similar to a worn-in tweed jacket. I think it actually got a bit softer with age. I am happy to report there is absolutely no pilling or loose threads.

My biggest pet peeve is saggy couch cushions. I cannot stand it when the fabric looks crumpled on the seats, and there are sloppy valleys on the back cushions. After having this sectional for four years, I can vouch that it still looks the same as the day we assembled it. Which is a small miracle because when the Range lived in the basement, it was base camp for elementary-age boys playing video games and jumping around. If for some reason you wanted to fluff, you can unzip the underside of the back cushions and take out the filling to give it more shape.

In terms of stains and spills, if any kids spilled something on the sofa, I don’t know about it because it has no markings. Come to think of it, I don’t think I’ve ever had to clean the sofa beyond brushing off crumbs.

I did catch my cat trying to stretch (scratch) on the back of the sectional a few times, but I shooed him away, and he did not make it a habit. When I checked, there were never any loops or snags. (I cannot say the same about another woven sofa that is a victim of his claws.)

The cushions are still in terrific shape.

The flexibility of the Burrow Range sectional is everything. That’s the main reason I would highly recommend this couch. Not only do the pieces come in individual boxes that can fit through narrow doorways of older homes, but you can customize the sectional to your exact needs.

Originally, I needed something to help with hosting my out-of-town family, but this sectional has proven again and again that it’s a high-quality piece that can hold up for years to come. I still can’t believe that the cushions are in tip-top shape.

Pricewise, it’s a solid buy for mid-range furniture, especially because I don’t see a reason to replace it any time soon. Even when I ended up getting a new green modular sectional to go with the new wallpaper that I installed during my basement makeover, I found a spot for it in my bedroom. The Range now serves as a reading nook or a makeshift WFH station when I don’t want to stay in bed but feel too lazy to walk down the stairs to my home office. I added a Häti pouf with a scalloped EtúHome board next to the Burrow ottoman, and it serves as a perch for my coffee.

All in all, I am very happy with this purchase. It is durable, comfortable, and boasts clean lines and a silhouette that is approachable, but a bit more interesting than a standard traditional sofa.

#6862. Why Taylor Swift Hasn’t Been Seen at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs-Broncos Game in Denver

Taylor Swift has attended all of Travis Kelce’s home games this year, but during the Kansas City Chiefs’ away game against the Denver Broncos today, the singer wasn’t seen at Empower Field.

Swift was out earlier in the day in New York City, where she participated in a Q&A during a Toy Story 5 screening. She wrote the film’s song “I Knew It, I Knew You,” which has Oscar buzz.

Swift hasn’t been spotted at any of Kelce’s away games for the past two seasons, with security risks reportedly factoring into the decision. The tight end has a home game next Sunday, though, so she could be out in full force to support him and his teammates then as they face off against the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium.

While she has regularly attended Kelce’s games throughout their three-year relationship, Swift has never deliberately drawn attention to her appearances. As she told Time in December 2023, “I’m just there to support Travis. I have no awareness of if I’m being shown too much and pissing off a few dads, Brads, and Chads.”

“I don’t know how they know what suite I’m in,” she added. “There’s a camera, like, a half-mile away, and you don’t know where it is, and you have no idea when the camera is putting you in the broadcast, so I don’t know if I’m being shown 17 times or once.”

Last year, Swift attended some of Kelce’s games without being photographed. Over the course of her career, she has mastered the art of entering and leaving places undetected. In an October 2025 interview with Scott Mills on BBC Radio 2, she revealed that this would be her greatest asset as a spy.

“Just put me in a garbage can, roll me, I don’t care,” she said. “Honestly, I can fit in like, a purse. Sometimes I just can’t deal with it [the paparazzi and attention] and in those times, I won’t deal with it. I’m just digging tunnels under every building I go into, airlifting in through the skylight.”

#6854. House Party: Angelica Hicks

With a new Paperless Post collection, the illustrator shares her rules for a party worth RSVPing yes to.

Welcome to House Party, where we ask expert hosts for their top entertaining tips, tricks, and tabletop tactics. Come party with us.

Angelica Hicks has a talent for making high fashion out of everyday materials. The British artist, illustrator, and fashion satirist is known for using household supplies to recreate runway and red-carpet looks, capturing couture’s most elaborate details with candy wrappers and duct tape. A sharp eye runs in the family: Her father is the artist and interior designer Ashley Hicks, and her grandfather was the influential decorator David Hicks. But her visual wit is distinctly her own, evident in everything from her illustrative book Tongue in Chic to her collaborations with Gucci.

Her newly launched invitation collection for Paperless Post brings that humor to entertaining, with designs including a shrimp holding a martini. Hicks’s own hosting philosophy is similarly spirited, though she’s quite serious about a well-considered seating chart. For House Party, we asked her about the best parties she’s attended, the merits of an emergency ice delivery, and the extravagance she’d happily import from Japan.

ELLE Decor: What are your three essentials when hosting?

Angelica Hicks: A great invite that sets the tone before the event. A shrimp holding a martini inviting you to a cocktail party perhaps?

What’s your top entertaining/hosting tip?

People love to complain about placement, but I am pro placement. I think telling people where to sit, and actually spending time considering it, will only benefit the flow of conversation—especially when mixing people who might not already know each other. I think it’s a fabulous thing to do when hosting a dinner party.

Who, dead or alive, is coming to your dream dinner party?

Noël Coward, Joan Crawford, Aretha Franklin, Cristóbal Balenciaga.

Announcing dietary restrictions upon arrival.

If you could add one exorbitantly extravagant component to a party, what would it be?

I think I would fly in urchin from Japan if it were the season.

Who threw the best party you’ve ever attended?

Unemployed Magazine always throws an excellent Halloween party. What makes it so great is that they select one iconic person as a theme and everyone dresses up as that person or someone in the universe. Last year was Liz Taylor, and the year before was Princess Diana.

I'm ashamed to say I rarely bring anything. But once I have arrived, if I notice there is something missing, I will order it, which I think is far more helpful. A bag of ice can come in much more handy than a mid bottle of red.

What historic party would you have liked to have attended?

I think I would have had great fun dressing up for the Rothschild Surrealist Ball.

Buy too much wine; you'll probably go through it.

I don’t have a dishwasher, so I always lament the washing up.

Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.

#6852. Hailey Bieber and Gracie Abrams Are Both Wearing “Stardust Eyes,” Fall’s Prettiest Makeup Trend

The beauty look is soft, shimmery, and oh-so-celestial

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Halloween may be over, but Bazaar editors still can’t stop talking about some of the most viral beauty moments from the past weekend. Case in point? The ethereal, angelic look we’re calling “Stardust Eyes,” seen recently on supermodel Hailey Bieber and singer-songwriter and Chanel Coco Mademoiselle Crush Absolu ambassador Gracie Abrams during her Saturday Night Live performance.

Unlike other popular beauty looks worn on the 31st, the “Stardust Eyes” trend is as wearable as it is versatile, anchored by glowing skin, flushed cherub cheeks, glossy lips, and a wash of sheer silvery color across the lids and around the tear ducts. Bieber’s take on the trend paired the stunning eye look with a diffused nude lip and bright pink blush. Abrams’s look, created by celebrity makeup artist Emily Cheng for Chanel Beauty, leaned into an effortless, no-makeup-makeup approach.

Abrams wore two Halloween-inspired outfits for each SNL performance, starting with the song “Hit the Wall,” dressed in an angel costume inspired by a similar look worn by actress Claire Danes in the 1996 film Romeo + Juliet.

After prepping the star’s skin with Chanel’s Sublimage La Crème Texture Fine moisturizer and Sublimage La Crème Yeux eye cream to boost her glow, Cheng refined Abrams’s skin using a combination of the brand’s Les Beiges Healthy Glow Foundation and Serum Concealer in B20, Baume Essentiel Multi-Use Glow Stick in the shade Sculpting, along with layers of its Joues Contraste Powder Blush in shades 80 Jersey and 602 Rose Ruban. To capture the “Stardust Eye,” the artist reached for Chanel’s Stylo Yeux eyeliner and Les Beiges Healthy Glow Natural Eyeshadow Palette in Cool, then topped Abrams’s lid with the pearlescent Ombre Essentielle powder in 220 Blanc Perle for an otherworldly finish. Cheng kept the singer’s lips glowy and sparkly to match the rest of her beauty look, lining them with Le Crayon Lèvres in 162 Nude Brun before adding Chanel’s Rouge Coco Hydra Gloss in shade 432 Cristal.

With peak holiday and party looks on the horizon, we expect more inspiration for elevated, shimmery beauty looks to populate our For You Pages in the coming weeks.

#6851. Zoë Kravitz and Harry Styles Had Very Different Costumes for His Harryween Concerts

Harry Styles celebrated his Harryween shows this weekend, and he and his fiancée, Zoë Kravitz, got into the spirit.

On October 30, the singer performed the first of his two Halloween-themed concerts at New York City’s Madison Square Garden, where he wrapped up his 30-show residency on Saturday. The singer used his annual Harryween concert as an opportunity to pay homage to Elvis Presley and a past version of himself.

For his Presley-inspired look, Styles took the stage wearing a white bedazzled jumpsuit with colorful embellishments that featured a cobalt blue cape attachment and gold-trimmed sunglasses.

Kravitz watched from the audience and embraced a more traditional look in a red jacket and matching skirt, tights, and devil horns. She was joined by actress Riley Keough, who is Presley’s granddaughter. Keough was spotted filming the performance and dancing along to 2019’s “Watermelon Sugar.”

In addition to paying tribute to Presley’s stage wardrobe, Styles recreated his 2010 X Factor audition look, honoring the moment that launched his career. He was just 16 when he was on the show.

For his second Harryween show on October 31, Styles and Kravitz decided to pay homage to New York City. Styles wore a giant, fuzzy rat costume, complete with a giant foam slice of pizza, a nod to the city’s viral pizza rat.

Kravitz, meanwhile, dressed up as a takeout bag. The actress wore a white mini bubble dress with the instantly recognizable smiley and slogan printed on it. She finished the look with black kitten heels.

Styles first introduced Harryween in 2021 during his Love on Tour run, when he dressed as Dorothy from The Wizard of Oz for the first night and a Pierrot clown for the second. The following year, he channeled Danny Zuko from Grease for a Halloween performance in Los Angeles.

#6850. This Brand-New Illinois Farmhouse Was Designed to Look Hundreds of Years Old

The team at Buccellato Design and Architecture focused on incorporating heritage details and timeworn furnishings.

For Aimee and Kevin Buccellato, the best compliment they could receive about a project isn’t, “Wow, it looks so different in here.” It’s that a home looks like they haven’t changed a thing.

On a country road in Momence, Illinois, a beloved farmhouse stands as a timeworn landmark for the surrounding agricultural community. For the homeowners—a retired couple returning to their Midwestern roots—the property was as much a repository of memories as it was a place to create new ones. “Having grown up nearby, the property evoked a strong sense of memory and place,” says Aimee, who founded Buccellato Design and Architecture alongside her husband, Kevin. “At the outset of the project, and throughout, our clients wanted the new house to feel like it had always been there, so much so that perhaps the neighbors could be led to believe that the original house remained intact, yet amended by skillful renovation and discreet additions.”

It was an architectural sleight of hand rooted in a distinctly Midwestern philosophy: “Be good to the neighbors.” Alongside the Buccellatos, the couple approached the 6,000-square-foot rebuild with the restraint of preservationists and the imagination of storytellers. “Great care was taken to instill the home and outbuildings with a sense of history and rootedness, creating a home that feels as though it’s been part of this bucolic setting for centuries,” says Kevin of the project, which also included the restoration of the property’s original 19th-century barn and corn crib. “We drew inspiration from traditional farm complexes, where homesteads were added slowly over time, reconnecting the site with its Folk-Victorian-Farm-House and agricultural building roots.”

Inside, the narrative continues through antique white oak floors, salvaged beams, heritage florals, and rooms that borrow their palettes from the landscape. In the kitchen, a wall of windows replaces upper cabinetry, framing sunrise over the barn and walnut trees. The glass porch offers sweeping views of the Kankakee River, while a tucked-away speakeasy recalls the original farmhouse’s stone foundation.

For Kevin and Aimee, the guiding principle was a new construction home that felt “sensitive, not wasteful, polite, not ostentatious,” an exercise in knowing when architecture and interiors should defer to their surroundings. The result is a house with an invented past and a very real sense of belonging that does the Midwest—and the neighbors—proud.

FAST FACTSDesigner: Buccellato Design and ArchitectureLocation: Momence, IllinoisThe Space: A four-bedroom, four-and-a-half-bathroom home across 6,000 square feet

The entryway offers a fitting introduction to the home'’s carefully constructed sense of history, replete with nickel gap paneling, fumed and waxed antique white oak floors, and a light-filled staircase. Even the furnishings—including a vintage Persian rug and antique Jacobean gateleg table—suggest a collection acquired over generations.

Benjamin Moore’s Nelson Blue sets a serene backdrop for the sitting room, where traditional silhouettes and understated patterns make an easy pairing. “This room was designed to honor the history of this property and embody the love that our clients hold for this special place,” adds Aimee.

A tufted mohair sofa, realized in a rich umber, lends a sense of history, while an iconic feather lamp by Bunny Williams offers a reminder that even the most classic rooms benefit from a little irreverence.

In the kitchen, the Buccellatos traded upper cabinets for an expansive wall of windows overlooking the farmland, relocating the practical necessities to an adjacent dish room and larder. Salvaged white oak beams and barnboards overhead reinforce the home’s agricultural roots, while furniture-like cabinetry and leathered black quartzite countertops strike a timeless note.

With natural light pouring in from three sides, the dining room is what the Buccellatos describe as “peaceful, soft, and ethereal,” equally suited to both morning coffee and candlelit dinners. A dreamy mural wallpaper by Susan Harter references the property’s location along the Kankakee River, while formal seating lends a sense of occasion without sacrificing the home’s easygoing country charm.

Nestled among mature trees, the primary bedroom feels almost suspended in the surrounding landscape. The Buccellatos leaned into that sense of serenity with the palette. “It’s a dreamlike mix of earthy neutrals and pale blues that paints a serene backdrop for elegant details, vintage furnishings, and a delicate mix of subtle pattern,” adds Kevin.

A French country canopy bed, dressed in tailored Schumacher linen, takes center stage, while vintage-inspired furnishings and subtle pattern keep the room from feeling overly precious. An adjacent sitting room offers a place to read the morning paper or unwind with a cup of tea in the evenings.

In the vestibule, a little pattern goes a long way. A climbing floral from Schumacher in inky charcoal makes a charming counterpoint to the bedroom’s hushed palette, while a checked window bench is the ideal spot to read, giving the passageway purpose.

Pale blue walls and creamy millwork lend the primary bathroom an old-fashioned prettiness. A custom vanity introduces a tailored architectural element, while a Cowtan & Tout floral Roman shade softens the room’s more utilitarian details.

Designed as a playful respite for guests and future grandchildren, this bedroom plays off pattern and primary hues. “The red painted woodwork feels unexpected and cheerful against the blue-and-white wallpaper, striped rug, and patterned bedding,” says Aimee.

“The house and barn are nestled within nature and encircled by old-growth trees that offer a sense of place and belonging,” says Kevin of the home’s idyllic backdrop.

Founded by Aimee and Kevin Buccellato, Buccellato Design & Architecture is a practice marked by twenty-plus years of close collaboration, in architectural practice and in life. With projects on both coasts and throughout the country, the firm’s award-winning work reveals a dedication to craft, artistry, and detail. Achieved in partnership with clients, their projects reflect a purposeful sense of rootedness in the landscape and abiding devotion to beauty and the comfort of home.

The trio attended Jay-Z’s final show at SoFi Stadium

A little over a week ago, Jay-Z held the final shows of his Jay-Z 30 Tour at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, where he had the support of his wife, Beyoncé, at both back-to-back concerts.

Even Queen Bey’s mom, Tina Knowles, came out to watch.

For her part, the pop superstar wore a bone-colored set from the LaPointe Spring/Summer 2027 ready-to-wear collection, which consisted of a sheer wrap top layered underneath a cropped jacket and paired with matching boyshorts, both of which were decorated with silver gemstones.

As for Blue Ivy, she wore a striped baseball top tucked into cutoff jean shorts, and she accessorized with Timberland boots, frameless sunglasses, and a black bandana nestled into her pocket.

#6847. Everything You Need to Know About The CFDA Awards

Nominees and winners, celebrity attendees, and more

Tonight’s CFDAs are like the Oscars of American fashion. The biggest awards presentation of the year, the evening celebrates design talent and creativity here in New York and across the country. These honors are determined by the CFDA Fashion Awards Guild, an invitation-only voting body of industry peers—fashion editors and journalists, retail executives, stylists, influencers, and other industry professionals—many of whom will gather for the ceremony tonight at New York’s Museum of Natural History.

This year, highly anticipated categories include Womenswear Designer of the Year, whose nominees include both industry heavyweights like Michael Kors and younger talent like Diotima’s Rachel Scott. Google Shopping’s American Emerging Designer of the Year is also a hot category, with buzzy nominees like Emily Dawn Long, Colleen Allen, and Zane Li of Lii. There will also be a number of celebratory honorees, including Tory Burch, who will receive the Positive Change Award, and Anthony Vaccarello, departing creative director of Saint Laurent, who will be given the title International Designer of the Year.

The Council of Fashion Designers of America has guaranteed a star-studded event. Alongside host Keke Palmer, presenters include Lupita Nyong’o, Matt Damon, Naomi Osaka, Cole Escola, Demi Moore, and Cornelia Guest.

To brief you on all the necessary information ahead of the announcements, we’ve aggregated the nominees, awards, and relevant details surrounding them—and will be updating the list with the winners in real time.

This year’s roster of nominated designers spans generations of American design talent, and each has had a significant role in shaping what women’s fashion looks like today. Every nominee is returning. Khaite’s Catherine Holstein has won twice, in 2022 and 2023; Rachel Scott, now head of Proenza Schouler, won for Diotima in 2024; and Michael Kors won in 1999. (He’s also received a number of other honors, including the Lifetime Achievement Award, from the CFDA.) Tory Burch and Wes Gordon of Carolina Herrera have each been nominated in this category once before.

Based on the year he’s had, Zane Li of Lii is the front-runner in this category, which was won last year by Ashlynn Park of Ashlyn. So far in 2026, he has won the CFDA Fashion Fund and the Fashion Trust U.S. Ready-to-Wear Award; he was also a runner-up for the LVMH Prize. But he has competition: Julian Louie of the artistic label Aubero and Colleen Allen of the buzzy, Victorian-inspired eponymous brand were both nominated in the category last year and have each been named LVMH Prize finalists in recent years. Newcomers include Julia Ferentinos of Juju Vera, who has shot to prominence for her antique-inspired jewelry beloved by fashion It girls, and Emily Dawn Long, whose crochet hats and viral slogan tees made her a favorite among both the downtown set and the Instagram algorithm.

The menswear nominees are all familiar to this space. Ralph Lauren has won CFDA Awards in both menswear and womenswear, alongside the lifetime achievement recognition. Mexican American designer Willy Chavarria is also a returning winner; he received this award in 2023 and 2024. Thom Browne took it home for the fourth time in 2025. Public School won in 2014. Snyder has never won but has received multiple nominations.

The accessories category presents an interesting mix of nominees. The Olsen twins have won this award numerous times for the beloved bags and shoes from the Row. Raul Lopez of Luar has won twice, and he’s coming off a year of launching a buzzy handbag collab with MCM. Stuart Vevers won in 2017, and his affordable leather goods for Coach continue to capture shoppers’ attention across generations. As for the final two on the list—both modern minimalist jewelry designers—Ana Khouri has received multiple nominations in this category, while this is Sophie Buhai’s first nomination.

The Positive Change Award goes to Tory Burch.

The Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award goes to photographers Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin, typically referred to as Inez and Vinoodh.

The International Designer of the Year Award goes to Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, who exited the label this fall after a decade at its helm.

The Media Award in honor of Eugenia Sheppard goes to Eva Chen, vice president of fashion at Meta.

The Founder’s Award in honor of Eleanor Lambert goes to Linda Fargo, as the SVP fashion and store presentation director is celebrating three decades at Bergdorf Goodman.

The Isabel Toledo Board of Directors’ Tribute will be presented to Susan Cianciolo, for her RUN collection.

#6844. Samira Nasr’s November Editor’s Letter: On Performance

From Natalie Portman to the dream team of John Legend, Lynn Nottage, and Whitney White, this month’s issue is all about those whose art takes place in front of an audience

I’m writing this from Paris as the Spring 2027 shows are wrapping up. One glorious night, I had the chance to see Céline Dion during her residency at the Plénitude Arena. What really struck me about her performance was her unique ability to unite an entire stadium. It was just her up there—no background dancers—using her voice to bring us along on her journey. It was deeply moving. I was reminded of how vital performance can be. I’m sure there were people in the arena whose lives and experiences and politics differ from my own, but we could all come together to revel in the sheer joy of an incredible show.

That is the spirit in which we celebrate this issue’s theme, performance. A performer can entertain us, transport us, and, crucially, connect us.

Our cover star, Natalie Portman, photographed by Carlijn Jacobs and styled by our style director at large, Malina Joseph Gilchrist, has consistently transported us over the years with great performances. In the coming months, she will deliver two more, in Cathy Yan’s biting art-world satire, The Gallerist, and in Lena Dunham’s hyped new rom-com, Good Sex. Both reveal a lighter, more humorous, though by no means less committed side of Portman, and that’s by design. “Right now,” she tells our executive editor, Leah Chernikoff, she’s focusing on “a lot of joy. I think it’s both for myself and what I hope to offer an audience. There’s a lot of really heavy stuff going on … and so it does feel like the biggest service you can do right now as an artist is to deliver some joy.”

Elsewhere in this issue, I am thrilled to feature a range of dancers, musicians, writers, and actors whose work I have long revered. The dream team of John Legend, Lynn Nottage, and Whitney White came together in conversation to discuss their new stage adaptation of the classic American novel and film Imitation of Life, which also marks Legend’s first musical. “At the core, this is a story about the American dream, with all of its contradictions and complications,” says Nottage.

Sarah Hoover brings us the story of one of ballet’s great modern partnerships—American Ballet Theatre’s Isabella Boylston and James Whiteside—as they prepare to dance their final performances together. Boylston, who welcomed her first child this summer, returned to the barre six weeks after giving birth in order to be ready to partner with Whiteside before he retires next summer. “If I had to go onstage with him tonight in Swan Lake, with zero rehearsal, I’d still feel good about it,” Boylston tells Hoover.

When this issue is on newsstands, our podcast, The Good Buy, cohosted by Chernikoff and our executive digital director, Lynette Nylander, will be back for its fourth season, available wherever you get your podcasts and on YouTube, featuring another incredible lineup of folks whose style we’re obsessed with, including Paloma Elsesser and Kim Kardashian. Each episode is a reminder that getting dressed is the ultimate performance.

#6840. Michael Kors Still Believes in Magic

The New York native is marking his namesake brand’s 45th anniversary in style.

When Michael Kors thinks back to his 40th anniversary runway show in 2021, he remembers it fondly as a step toward a dream fulfilled. At the time, Covid restrictions had kept audiences from viewing the collection in person, though supermodels like Naomi Campbell and Bella Hadid walked the show, turning New York’s Theater District into a runway. “It was a bit of wishful thinking about how life would be once the city reopened,” Kors says. “Even though we were shut down, I knew that eventually the city would revitalize—and now life has not only returned, it’s returned with a vengeance.”

Five years later, dreams became reality as he hosted his 45th anniversary fall 2026 runway show in one of New York’s most famous cultural landmarks, the Metropolitan Opera House, at Lincoln Center this past February. His return to a theatrical venue marked a full-circle moment, a celebration of life lived in community with others. Kors recalled a recent trip to the opera house where young women in attendance were dressed to the nines, which for Kors was a clear sign of a post-Covid affinity for glamour. “People are celebrating going out, and they want to look great while they’re doing it,” Kors says. “This 45th anniversary show was a love letter to live performance, to New York City, and to going out and making an entrance.” The collection more than lived up to that promise, with leather opera gloves and draped evening dresses. In a fitting throwback, Christy Turlington—who starred in the designer’s first ad campaign—closed the show. Broadway stars like Rachel Zegler and Nicole Scherzinger watched from the front row before heading across the street to another Manhattan institution, P.J. Clarke’s, to celebrate with champagne toasts and a serenade from Rufus Wainwright.

For Kors, famously a patron of the arts, choosing the space as a backdrop for his collections was intentional. Live performance and fashion have always been connected for him, particularly through movement. Just as a performance changes when experienced through a screen, clothes lose something when reduced to a still image. That idea was central to the brand’s 45th anniversary collection. “We don’t live in a still picture, we live in a moving video,” he says. The transporting power of live performance is worth fighting for, particularly as financial support for the arts has been faltering. “We have very few times in our lives when we are in a communal situation,” Kors says. “Anything that allows us to unplug and experience something magical with other human beings is something we can’t let disappear.”

There is another somewhat fantastical engine that fuels Kors: New York. Throughout the brand’s history, he has captured the essence of the city’s dynamic style. “New York is always changing,” the designer says. “The energy has always been a source of inspiration.” Describing the city’s fashion scene as “contradictory,” even comparing it to a “big bowl of potato chips with caviar,” Kors understands the balance between function and glamour, discipline and indulgence. This dance between those opposing impulses is what gives New York its unmistakable character. “When things are strictly casual, it feels boring, and when they’re strictly glamorous, it feels too special for daily life.”

That balance of ease and enchantment has been foundational to the Kors brand since its inception. In a review of the brand’s first runway show in 1984, WWD defined the collection as “haute, classic streetwear” and “elegant but minimal,” sentiments that the designer still identifies with today. “When I read things that were said about me when I first started, you would say, ‘Wow, he’s still using that same playbook,’ and I am.” But while his design ethos has remained steady, Kors is sympathetic to how culture, and thus fashion, has drastically changed. “What is considered casual now versus what was considered casual in the ’80s? Night and day.” From how clothes were designed to how they were styled, the differences were drastic. “When I started,” he points out, “there were no stretch fabrics—jeans didn’t stretch.”

To the untrained eye, Kors’s staple designs, like a camel trench coat, a hand-knit black cashmere sweater, or a flattering red dress, may seem simple. But each design, fabric, and color choice is laced with deep sentimentality. “I love anything that has the possibility of interpretation,” Kors says. “When it comes to color, black is limitless for a designer, and as far as bright colors, red is always what I go to. Red is life-affirming.”

When Kors thinks back on where it all began, his mind goes to Studio 54. He skipped his high school prom to go to the famed disco, and says that was the night that he knew he wanted to be a fashion designer. “Seeing people move in their clothes, feel confident, understand their own sensuality—that was something you saw at Studio 54,” he says. “It really represented the best thing about New York: the mix of people. People from every background, every language, all together in this magical space. And the cool thing was that there was no social media and no judgment, so people could truly let go and have a good time.” Kors is acutely aware of a cultural craving for togetherness and community. Through his designs and runway shows, he aims to highlight the beauty, comfort, and even theatricality that come with living life authentically with one another. Studio 54 has since been turned into a theater, and Kors relishes, once again, New York’s ability to reinvent itself. Voilà: magic.

#6839. The Surprise It: Welcome to Derry Episode Is Crawling with Stephen King Lore

HBO dropped a special Halloween episode over the weekend, which tells the origin story behind the origin story.

You might want to keep some of your Halloween decorations up a bit longer, because there’s a treat still hiding at the bottom of your candy bag. While everyone was out trick-or-treating on Saturday, October 31, HBO released a surprise new episode of It: Welcome to Derry. And yes, it’s scary, spooky, and very much worth watching. Especially for Stephen King lorehounds.

Titled It: Welcome to Derry — A Story of Derry, the special episode is a standalone prequel that reveals how the Sqoteawapskot locked Pennywise away in the forests of Derry. It is framed as the “real” story, unsanitized by the “gentler tale” that the Sqoteawapskot tribe cooked up for the sake of the children. “This is the story we do not teach,” reads the introduction text. “This is the part we left out.”

Kiawentiio (Avatar: The Last Airbender) reprises her role as Neekani, who previously appeared through flashbacks in season 1. But in A Story of Derry, Neekani is now the main protagonist. She defies her elders to hunt in the forbidden Western Wood and help replenish their dwindling food supply.

For most of the special, Neekani and her friends brave their encounter with “It”—also the Gallo—who is growing more powerful now that it’s feasting on English settlers. There’s also a creepy dude named Mitig (played by Zahn McClarnon) who is the first to learn that the shards of It’s giant crystal ship can ward the monster away. There’s also a predictable but nasty plot twist involving Mitig’s true motives, which I won’t give away.

But the real draw is the live-action debut of a pretty important character from Stephen King’s mythos: Maturin. He appears to Neekani after she smokes some of Mitig’s herbs, and he informs her how her tribe can contain It for at least a few generations.

A character from both It and King’s The Dark Tower series, Maturin is a benevolent turtle-like deity powered by “The White.” His goodness, purity, and light stand in opposition to It’s darkness. He has a small but pivotal role in the novel, telepathically communicating with Bill and protecting the children during the Ritual of Chüd. He dies at some point after choking on a universe. Which kind of feels like a joke on the part of Stephen King, given that turtles don’t chew.

A Story of Derry is the quickest half hour you might spend this week. It’s a solid piece of American Indian horror, which remains a criminally rare occurance throughout mainstream pop culture. (The closest I can think of is 2022’s Prey, which is barely a horror flick, though A Story of Derry feels cut from the same cloth.) There are heavy allusions to the traumas of colonization, as well as the loss of land and way of life.

While Bill Skarsgärd doesn’t appear as Pennywise, sadly, “It” puts on a scary face as a creepy, pox-riddled Christian missionary who taunts Neekani’s mother. Still, like a bar of Twix at the bottom of a trick-or-treat pail, A Story of Derry is a most welcome surprise. Now we’re left wondering when season 2 will premiere. What’s the over/under on a Christmas surprise?

#6837. 33 Gifts for Wives Who Hope You've Been Listening

One of the great pleasures of being married is bearing witness to your life partner's tastes and obsessions. And you'd think all that inside knowledge would make buying her a gift a cinch, and yet here you are, looking up the best gifts for wives. No judgment—we've been there. Whether it's an anniversary, a birthday, or just an occasion to remind her how much you appreciate her, we've rounded up a few things that have been on our radar all year. And yes, you should probably make that dinner reservation, too.

Still got names on your list? We've got ideas. Peruse the rest of our gift guides, and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a regular dispatch of things we think are worth your money.

It's easy to get distracted by all the excellent cashmere at Banana, but the brand knows its way around silk, too. This shirt is cut roomy and relaxed, with the sort of effortless drape that makes getting dressed easy.

Coach's Empire Carryall comes in a whole family of sizes, all cut from the brand's soft glovetanned leather. It's a beautiful bag on its own, but I'd suggest picking out a few charms to dangle from the handles to make it hers.

Phoebe Philo's Peak sunglasses are aptly named: the shape is, quite simply, peak. An absolute stunner of a pair, and just imagine her walking into brunch wearing them.

Depending on whom you ask, the Moon Shoe might just be Nike's defining sneaker of the moment. Credit Jacquemus, whose collaboration turned a relic of the brand's running history into one of fashion's most coveted shoes.

J.Crew has barn jackets on the brain this year, and its considerable efforts might just have you lusting after one yourself. I'm partial to the studded version, but there's plenty to choose from, including corduroy and faux shearling renditions.

A silk scarf is an endlessly good gift, if only because there are endless ways to wear one. Around her neck, in her hair, knotted onto a handbag, however she pleases, really.

Brooches are all over the runways right now, and might just be the easiest way to lend an outfit a little extra panache. This dangly little number from Lie Studio features carnelian stone, with a rich, brownish-red hue that feels of the moment.

A coworker Chris first put me onto Simuero, but it wasn't until a trip to Barcelona earlier this year that I got to see the Spanish jewelry label's work in person, at Bassal Store. Beautiful stuff, with an organic, slightly imperfect quality that's even better up close.

This is about as chic as it gets, as far as under-eye patches go. The silky patches promise a little firming power, and the set also includes the Le Lift hand cream as an extra treat.

Makeup, of course, is a tricky thing to gift, but a colleague of mine showed up to the office wearing this purple blush from Violette_FR, and I was immediately sold on the shade. I've had it on my running list of recommendations ever since.

Soft Services has shrunk its beloved exfoliating Buffing Bar down to miniature proportions, with four little bars in a very giftable set. A posh way to keep skin in check, and low-key great for travel.

There was plenty of oohing and aahing when a small sample of Maison Francis Kurkdjian's Oud Velvet Mood landed on my desk this year. A gorgeous oud with notes of peach, suede, and leather.

Dr. Sturm has built quite a following for her science-minded approach to skincare. This travel-friendly set brings together some of her signature formulas, all tucked into a fuzzy fleece bag.

Sidia's Braless Duo pairs a subtly scented mist and serum, a welcome salve for winter-weary skin.

Rocco's game-changing beverage fridge now has a more affordable sibling. The Essential holds more than 100 cans and costs considerably less than the flagship Super Smart Fridge, while retaining the same compressor.

One floral and bittersweet, the other peachy and citrus-forward, these botanical aperitivi are deliciously complex without trying to taste like booze. Serve over ice or topped with soda.

Caraway isn't the first to make a coffee maker with an all-glass-and-steel brewing system, keeping hot coffee away from plastic. But it might just be the best-looking of the bunch, which counts when it's one of the first things they see in the morning.

What, your dinner parties don't involve serving salad with horn-handled, mother-of-pearl spoons? Gohar's nautilus shell-inspired salad servers are spectacularly unnecessary, which is why they make such a great gift.

Hario might be best known for its coffee gear, but the Japanese brand knows its way around matcha, too. This gift set includes a double-walled glass bowl and everything she needs to prepare a prower bowl of matcha.

Just the thing to christen that new matcha set. Kettl sources its teas directly from growers, and I'm currently taken with its Okuju matcha. Developed with a longtime partner in Uji, Japan's storied tea-growing region just outside Kyoto, it's a particularly fine powder with a delicate nuttiness and a wonderfully smooth finish.

Edie Parker's gemstoned lighter case has long been a go-to gift around these parts, but this year we've got our eye on the matching ashtray. No smoking equired—it makes a pretty fab catchall for jewelry, keys, and other little things.

I love the freaky pop-art vibes of this collaboration between Dusen Dusen and Venetian glassmaker Laguna~B. The pitcher is great on its own, but you can also spring for the set with two matching glasses.

Apple's new AirPods 5 come in two tiers, and the more giftable of the two is the version with the wireless charging case. You get longer battery life and swipe-to-adjust volume controls right on the stems.

For the record collector, U-Turn's Orbit Plus is one of the finest midrange turntables around. This version has a built-in phono preamp, so she can get straight to spinning records with a pair of powered speakers.

Taking its cues from Kodak's '70s-era 110 camera, Camp Snap offers a screen-free digital experience with an 8MP sensor, which is modest by today's standards, but entirely the point.

Nothing says great gift quite like an overengineered personal fan she'd never buy herself. Dyson's bladeless design is the clever bit, delivering a steady stream of air that's whisper-quiet.

If she's going to track her health, she might as well do it with the latest Oura Ring. The fifth-gen model is 40% smaller, with more proactive insights and personalized guidance to help her make sense of all that data.

Electric toothbrushes aren't exactly paragons of sustainable design, but Suri is doing its damnedest to change that. Its Pro 2.0 has recyclable plant-based brush heads, a repairable body, and a rechargeable battery designed to keep the whole thing out of a landfill for longer.

How could Theragun possibly improve on its already excellent mini massage gun, you ask? By adding heat, of course. The Mini Plus combines percussive massage with warming therapy to help loosen up sore muscles.

If cupping is good enough for the sporting elite, it's certainly worth a spot in her recovery routine. Wthn's kit includes eight silicone cups for a gentler take on the practice that can still help relieve muscle tension.

Wonder Valley's hinoki-scented bath products have won over a few of GQ's more relaxation-minded staffers. This set pairs a handsome bar of soap with a sachet of bath tea, which can be steeped a few times before it's finally spent.

Red-light technology is coming for sex toys, and Lelo's Mona Spectra is among the first to get in on the action. Expect to see plenty more of it in the years ahead, but there's nothing wrong with being an early adopter in this particular department.

#6834. The 11 Best Fragrances Released This October

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The new smoky, spicy scents you need to know about.

I love fragrance. I love fall. Put the two together, and I’m in olfactory heaven. I’ve been excited to put this roundup together since the first new spooky scents started hitting shelves early last month—as we get into November, it’s evident that October will be a tough one to follow up.

There’s plenty of spice and smoke in the air, plus rich gourmands that feel tailor-made for colder weather. There’s even a new fragrance collection in partnership with Robert Eggers’s latest gothic horror film, for anyone who’s ever wanted to smell like they could turn into a werewolf at any moment—or, well, just want to smell like they’ve been at a bonfire. Ready to find your next fall scent? Read on for 11 exciting new fragrances you can get now.

If you’re looking for a new go-to fragrance for fall and winter, let it be Commodity Spice. Like a hot cup of chai, this expressive fragrance is warm and smooth with a rich cocktail of spices including saffron, nutmeg, clove, cardamom, and cinnamon. If I close my eyes, I feel like I just stepped into a cozy little tea and spices shop, and I want to wear that feeling like a sweater.

When Fulton & Roark released Cathedral of Ruins, it quickly became one of our favorite cold-weather smoky scents. Not only does it have a super unique aroma of smoldering frankincense, black pepper, rose, and woods, but it has a heartbreakingly beautiful origin story—the brand’s founders were inspired to create the scent after visiting the abandoned City Methodist Church in Gary, Indiana. The fragrance is an homage to the religious rituals that once took place in that church.

Think of a buttery croissant; a butterscotch candy; a cinnamon roll with sweet, creamy frosting. Those are the vibes of Gap’s newest fragrance. A late addition to the newly (re)launched collection of EDPs, it joins the group as the first gourmand—just in time for fall. Oh, and if you like how Bliss smells, you can complete the collection with the scented hand cream and body lotion.

I was always under the impression that fruity fragrances and woody ones had very little to do with each other and that, for the most part, they should stay separate. That’s until I smelled Maison d’Etto’s Pinehurst. Here, fruity notes of rambutan, blood orange, and ripe pineapple provide a beautiful overlay to base notes of leather, oud, and other woods. It’s a radiant scent that works year-round, day and night.

David Moltz (the “D.S.” of D.S. & Durga) was inspired to create this Resurrected Corpse Flower fragrance after visiting the Brooklyn Botanical Garden during the height of a rare blooming of a corpse flower. What he smelled was, in his words, “like a baby diaper pail in a rotten fish tank full of rubber lily bulbs & olives.” But then he got to thinking, what if that scent could be cleaned of all its rotten odors and reborn into something beautiful? Thus, Resurrected Corpse Flower was born. With green olive, lily, tuberose, freesia, and deep bog cedar, it’s a truly special scent that’s at once floral and swampy.

Because this fragrance is so unlike anything I’ve ever smelled before, it might be a bit polarizing; I’m sure some of you will love it, and others might prefer one of D.S. & Durga’s other unique fragrances. But after leaving this scent on my skin for a bit, I really started to appreciate it.

In contrast to some of the deep, rich gourmands on this list, Lumira’s Soléor offers a lighter, sun-soaked gourmand option. Instead of creamy sweetness, it’s more of a soft, sensual sweetness that isn’t too heavy or overpowering. Smooth amber and candied fruit up top give it a bit of a citrusy kick, which fades into caramel, vanilla, and woods. It works for fall and winter just as well as it does for spring and summer.

If you do want something rich and creamy, Phlur’s Heavy Cream is the way to go. It’s an ambery gourmand with notes of vanilla mousse, white orchid, and creamy musk, which are balanced out by hints of sparkling lemon and orange flower, adding a little bit of lightness to the otherwise heavy fragrance. And, of course, with a name like Heavy Cream, there has to be a coordinating whipped body butter for the full experience.

How do you make decadence refined? You create a rich, vanilla gourmand and add the sophisticated warmth of Peru balsam. It’s definitely a sweet scent, and the combination of Cristal vanilla, bourbon vanilla, tonka bean, and black sugar creates the aroma of a classic crème brûlée. But once you get past the creamy sweetness of it all, you’re left with a sensual, balsamic scent that lingers.

I didn’t know a fragrance could smell so much like Halloween, but Heretic teamed up with Robert Eggers’ new movie Werwulf and did just that. At first, you get spice and smoke from cardamom, smoke, and leather; it then moves into something woody, earthy, and animalic with fir balsam, labdanum, patchouli, moss, and damp earth. The “suggestion of wet fur” is what really makes this scent stand out—and what gives it that spooky edge. Wear with your scariest Halloween costume.

In a departure from the mostly spicy, rich, gourmand scents that hit shelves this October, Drake’s Better World Fragrance House partnered with October’s Very Own for a fresh, citrusy fragrance that gives the impression of a refreshing white wine sangria with notes of passion fruit, rose, white cedarwood, and roasted tonka bean. But in its spherical burgundy glass bottle, it’ll blend in perfectly with your other fall and winter scents.

Roll-on fragrance oils are all the rage right now, and new fragrance house Gamine has already come out with its own collection of fragrance oils called Microdose. With six parfum oils, you can wear each individually or combine two or three for your own unique scent. My favorite of the bunch is DMT, a metallic fragrance built on notes of burnt latex, aerated foam, and hot steel. I wasn’t sure I would like it based on the description—and the fact that I’d never heard of a metallic scent before—but I’m actually obsessed with it.

#6833. The Author Behind the Pseudonym Rebecca Morrow Was a Total Mystery—Until Now

Rainbow Rowell is the bestselling writer behind the novel Corinne. Here, she explains why it was finally time to come forward.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In 2022, the novel Corinne was published. At the story’s center is Corinne, a woman who walked away from family and her fundamentalist upbringing but finds herself unable to forget Enoch, her first love. Rebecca Morrow, the name on the book’s cover, was described as a “pseudonym for a New York Times bestselling author,” and though readers guessed at who that author might be, Rebecca Morrow’s identity remained a mystery until now.

Rebecca Morrow is Rainbow Rowell, the celebrated author of Cherry Baby and Eleanor & Park, among others. Corinne isn’t about her life, but it has parallels, and in 2022, publishing something so personal felt impossible. Now denying what she has come to consider her favorite book seems unthinkable. In July 2027, Corinne will be reissued with Rowell’s name on the cover, and in 2028 she will publish Catch Us the Foxes, a Corinne sequel.

Here Rowell talks about the decision to write Corinne—and deciding to finally put her name on it—in her own words.

In the darkest hours of the COVID-19 pandemic—when the future seemed uncertain, and the rest of the world felt far away—I did something very strange for me.

I wrote a book, knowing that I couldn’t let anyone read it.

“I just need to do this,” I told my literary agent. “And then I’ll write something we can sell.” It was a good time to sell. I’d just published three No. 1 bestsellers in a row. “I just need to get this out of me first.”

I wrote the first draft of the novel almost feverishly. It was about a woman who is cast out of her strict Christian church as a teenager and cut off by her family. She comes back home as an adult to reckon with the past—and with the man who was the catalyst for her exile.

Really, the book was about all the things I’d always been too scared to write about, or even to talk about….Faith. Shame. Sex. (More sex. Unclean sex. Forbidden sex. Sex in the same room as a Bible.) And, most thornily, how it feels to leave a fundamentalist church. The way you eventually realize that you can’t leave. That you’ll always take it with you, because you were made there. Baked there. Poured and set.

When I was done with the manuscript, it was my favorite thing I’d ever written. Maybe not my best book, but already the one I loved the most.

“But honestly,” I told my agent, “we can’t do anything with this. It’s too personal. And it’s the very last thing any of my readers would want.” I was writing queer YA fantasy. Not whatever this was.

My agent, being an agent, asked if he could read it anyway.

And he liked it. (He liked my beautiful baby!)

We very quickly began talking about a way to publish the book that might sidestep all my fears and anxieties….

There began my strange—and still hardly believable to me—journey as Rebecca Morrow, the pseudonymous author of Corinne.

It was exciting at first. It was different and fun. A pseudonym! A secret identity! A way to drop a novel into the world without having to talk about it, or sell it. Without having to worry about alienating or recruiting my existing readers.

The pseudonym satisfied that still feverish part of me that needed to let the story out, but was too terrified to stand by it.

Oh, I knew it was absurd to write a book about shame and secrets, and then to keep it a secret. (Don’t think this didn’t come up in therapy!) But at the time, it seemed like the only path forward for Corinne. It was this or let the characters die on my hard drive.

My editor and I agonized over how to handle the pseudonym. Traditionally, authors write fake biographies to go with their fake names. But I didn’t want to get caught in a lie if I was found out. And I didn’t want to seek out undeserved goodwill as a “debut author.”

The marketing department really wanted something they could say about Rebecca Morrow. They suggested “lives in Nebraska,” but even that felt like divulging too much. We settled on “Rebecca Morrow is a pseudonym for a New York Times bestselling author.”

My apologies to the bestselling, usually Mormon, authors who got blamed for this weird book. I didn’t see that coming.

I did expect readers to guess that I was the author. Even though I’d freed myself to write Corinne in a new voice and shaken off some of my more recognizable habits, the book ended up sounding more like me than ever. It was like my voice distilled.

Some people did guess. It didn’t bother me. I still didn’t have to talk about the book. I didn’t have to face it.

Corinne is my favorite of my books and beyond that, Enoch and Corinne, the man and woman at its center, are my all-time favorite characters. It’s hard to explain why…

I always write messy, flawed characters, but these two are my messiest and most flawed. Their love is not the stuff of romance. (This novel is not a romance; it will disappoint you if you come to it looking for reassurance or escape.)

Neither Corinne nor Enoch is based on me, though they carry many of my burdens. This is not a hidden memoir. But they feel so real to me. They make mistakes, and I want to forgive them. I want them to find grace. I think about them still, all the time. I worry about what’s become of them.

Ultimately, that’s why I’m stepping forward to claim the book now. At some point, “not having to talk about Corinne” turned into “not being able to talk about Corinne,” even when I desperately wanted to.

I love this book! I want to put it on my shelf, between Any Way the Wind Blows and Scattered Showers. I want readers who liked Slow Dance and Cherry Baby to discover it.

I loved the characters in Corinne so much that I wrote a sequel about them—Catch Us the Foxes—and I want that book to have a life, too. William Morrow is launching both books, properly—Corinne next July, and Catch Us the Foxes in March 2028—in beautiful hardcover editions.

I revised Corinne for the new edition—I went a little deeper on the church stuff this time, and sharpened the focus on some of the characters. It’s a little longer. And, I think, a little better. My favorite designer, Jim Tierney, designed the new matching covers.

I still get a surge of fear and excitement every time I see my name there front and center.

My therapist says that I’m very good at compartmentalizing—keeping some parts of myself shut away from other parts. I would argue that this is a very useful skill! But it does bad things to your soul, over time...being fractured like that.

But as the years have passed, it’s felt like I’ve left something half done. Like Corinne is a truth half shared. A story half told. I needed to get the book out of me, but I ended up cutting myself off from it. That was never the goal.

I’m grateful to “Rebecca Morrow” for making Corinne possible, but I’m finally ready to bring these characters home.

#6831. 4 Epic New Watches Every Watch Guy Is Salivating Over Right Now

Welcome to Watch Guy Watches, GQ’s monthly curation of high-end timepieces for the true watch nerds among us. This month, Moser goes retro(grade); Lange brings back a beloved bracelet; Biver drops its first hand-wound three-hander; and Breitling puts a pair of vintage-inspired watches in its core catalog.

There are only a few firm absolutes in the horological sphere. One of them is “never bet against H. Moser & Cie.” The high-end independent maker never ceases to amaze with its creativity, wit, and technological prowess. From a mechanical timepiece that bears a suspicious resemblance to a certain famous smartwatch to one the coolest integrated bracelet-bearing luxury sports watches on the market, Moser consistently delivers the Swiss-made goods.

Building upon its Pioneer Retrograde Seconds Midnight Blue release from two years ago, three new models with retrograde seconds join the collection this month in the Pioneer, Endeavour, and Streamliner collections. While all three are beautiful, however, it’s the latter whose aesthetics pair particularly well with this steampunk-esque complication—one in which a small hand tracks the passing seconds in an arc and then jumps back to its starting position at the top of each 30-second period.

Housed in a 40mm brushed stainless steel cushion case with a serpentine integrated bracelet, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds offers a potent mix of Streamline Moderne and futurism before one even considers its dial. Executed in midnight blue fumé enamel, it features applied indices and the brand’s signature modified syringe handset, with a faint “H. Moser & Cie” signature appearing in white beneath 12 o’clock. The lower half of the face, meanwhile, is given over to the retrograde seconds display. Inspired by instrument gauges such as automotive speedometers, it features smooth action powered by the cal. HMC 252, a product of movement specialists Agenhor. (Flip the watch over and you can view its tungsten rotor whirring away via a sapphire caseback.)

One of the coolest features of the Streamliner collection is that despite the presence of numerous complications; of the use of fumé dials; and of high-end pricing, these watches are meant to be used. With 120m of water resistance, steel constriction, automatic winding, and 72 hours of power reserve, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds is effectively a high-end tool watch. (Though at a sticker price of 29,900 CHF, maybe take it off if you’re, like, climbing Mt. Everest or whatever?)

While retrograde seconds displays don’t have the same utility as calendar readouts or GMT complications, they do demonstrate horological competence on the part of the watchmaker…and more importantly, they’re wild fun to watch in action. And if you can’t have a little fun in your watch-collecting journey, well—then what the heck are you even doing here, anyway?!

If you’ve been waiting years for the return of platinum bracelet options for A. Lange & Söhne’s Datograph Perpetual watch, we give you permission to rejoice: a new version of the timepiece—made in honor of the model’s 20th anniversary—is equipped not only with a diamond-studded black dial, but with a fresh matching platinum bracelet. Designed with five links rather than the seven of early-2000s models made by German jewelry manufacturer Wellendorff, said bracelet is perhaps more notable than the watch itself, which features the brand’s manually wound manufacture Calibre L952.1 movement and is limited to just 50 pieces.

When watch-world elder statesman Jean-Cladue Biver and his son Pierre co-founded their eponymous firm in 2022, their introductory product was a half-million-dollar automatic tourbillon and minute repeater. Having since added a simple automatic three-hander to their lineup in the form of the Automatique, they’re now expanding their offerings with a hand-wound three-hander in stainless steel. Dubbed the AB, it measures 38mm wide and 9.8mm tall and features a beautiful black multi-level onyx dial with gold accents, plus a cool stainless steel bracelet with an angular five-link design and a patented micro-adjust system. Powered by the new Calibre JCB-004 designed in collaboration with Le Cercle des Horlogers, it’s the brand’s entry-level model…though it’ll still set you back roughly the cost of a BMW M3. (Naturally, it’s already sold out.)

On the slightly less eye-watering—but no less compelling—end of the watch-guy spectrum is the new Breitling Navitimer B09 Chronograph 41. Why does it look so familiar, you might ask? Effectively, it’s a modern version of the famed ref. 806 “Twin Jet”-logo chronograph from the 1960s, only this time, it’s available as a non-limited edition—a fact that will surely excite deep Breitling aficionados. Measuring 41mm in stainless steel, it’s manually wound just like its vintage namesake, and comes paired to a brown leather strap for $7,900 or to a handsome steel bracelet for $8,400. If you fancy something a bit more left-field, there’s also a hand-wound, non-limited version of the Cosmonaute, a riff on the Navitimer equipped with a 24-hour dial that was famously worn by astronaut Scott Carpenter in 1962 ($10,600-$11,000).

#6828. Vince Staples Is Our November 2026 Music Director

The rapper crafts an exclusive playlist for Bazaar that ranges from songs from his childhood to songs that show the vastness of what hip-hop can be

Vince Staples is known for his matter-of-fact, bluntly honest lyrics. The California-born rapper often taps into the realities of Long Beach, his hometown, meditating on urban poverty, systemic racism, and even skepticism of the music industry. This lyricism emerges from the rapper’s desire to remain authentic and has been evident throughout his career from his 2015 debut, Summertime ’06.

“Whatever your viewpoint on life is or whatever you’re experiencing at this current moment is going to translate into the music that you create, no matter what,” Staples told Bazaar in an interview this summer. “As you get older, you learn to embrace that.”

The musician, 33, did exactly that on his seventh studio album, Crybaby, an urgent, politically charged record that trades traditional beats for post-punk melodies. He confronts historical racism on songs like “Tulsa, OK” and “Cotton” while indicting the entertainment industry for continuing to incite racism against Black people in songs like “TV Guide.” Other songs tap directly into his experience, like “White Flag,” which reflects on his personal journey as an artist and entertainer.

“I want to come up with the idea that feels most organic,” he says, adding that he never listens to music when he’s in the writing process. “I don’t like to be inspired by other music,” he says. “I feel like it’s a disservice to the lives that we live every day…. Music reminds you of what you experience in your life, and it forces you to look inward.” This same instinct guided Staples as he assembled the playlist for Bazaar’s Performance issue, compiling songs that have been foundational to him as an artist and performer.

He often admires introspective songwriting. Blu’s track “Vanity,” featured on the California rapper’s album Her Favorite Colo(u)r (2011), reminds him of the personal, diaristic storytelling style that influenced his early works. “The way he tells stories, it’s the way that I really got into hip-hop music for myself,” he recalls. Today, he cites his friend Steve Lacy’s ability to capture a “good adaptation of his thoughts at the current moment” with “Nice Shoes,” the lead single from the album Oh Yeah? Staples, reflecting on how personal music is, suggests that songs “all have to mean something to us for them to even come to mind” in the first place.

Given the artist’s relationship to music, Staples chose songs that reminded him of moments in his life. One of the album’s oldest tracks is Ray Charles’s soulful “Drown in My Own Tears,” which hearkens back to his childhood. “[Ray Charles] has been ever-present in my life because growing up as a Black person in America and Southern California with older parents or older grandparents, he would be a fixture in music, whether it’s country music, soul music, R&B, music—you can put him in a lot of those different subgenres, but just as far as black music in general,” he says.

Another staple of American Black music is James Brown, but Staples decided to include the Who’s muscular 1965 cover of Brown’s “I Don’t Mind.” For him, the song offers a lesson in transformation and reinterpretation, telling Bazaar it “unearthed the idea of coverage and the ecosystem of sharing music or repurposing music.” On his new album, for instance, he samples Slick Rick’s “Children’s Story” on his song “The Big Bad Wolf.”

In this way, Staples inherently views music as an expansive medium. He recalls how recently the Beastie Boys song “Sabotage,” a buoyant mixture of rap and hardcore punk, helped him explain to a friend “the vastness of what we consider to be hip-hop music.” Ultimately, for Staples, a song’s ability to change you makes it indelible. “It’s a testament to what it meant to you in the moment you first heard it,” he says. “Having that brought back to the forefront is a cool part of the process.”
