#6826. 7 Celebrity Outfits You Should Steal This Month

With the holidays looming and next year’s awards season on the horizon, there’s no rest for the A-list weary. Between hitting up screenings, press junkets, and the general business of being a star, you’ll occasionally catch famous folks kicking their feet up in suites at SoFi Stadium or risking a courtside collision with a referee at an NBA game.

From Harry Styles getting his heart rate up on morning runs over the Williamsburg Bridge to Ethan Hawke turning up for a SAG screening, Glenn Close pulling an absolute grail piece from a film she starred in alongside Robert Redford, and Nicholas Hoult hopping between planes, the celebrity style circuit is showing no signs of slowing down.

Maybe this is the season you’ve been influenced to go all in on corduroy, resurrect those vintage graphic tees gathering dust in your tote bins, or finally dip your dainty toes into the jazz shoe craze. Whatever your sartorial itch, let these celebrities do the legwork for you.

The Hawkester has worn corduroy before, and this look calls to mind Robin Williams in Dead Poets Society, whose affinity for the fabric felt like part of the curriculum. Hawke styles the suit in a way that feels less adjunct professor and more stoner student, thanks to a ratty graphic tee and tinted shades. Rather than dress shoes, he opts for well-worn dark brown Sambas, which contrast nicely with his acorn-colored suit. Carpe diem, and all that.

The star of Netflix’s upcoming show The Altruists demonstrates how dressing in a flowy, monochromatic palette doesn’t have to feel boring. The burgundy trench coat injects just enough color to keep things interesting. Leave it open so you don’t look like Inspector Gadget, and throw on tinted sunglasses, because they’re never a bad idea, no matter the fit.

With his Together, Together tour wrapping up at the end of the month, Harry’s New York stroll fits will likely be inducted into the annals of celeb big fits. He seems to have tapped into the lore of ’90s-era skaters, layering a long-sleeved tee under a T-shirt. Add light-wash jeans, all-white sneakers, and Apple earbuds, and you’ve got a man who feels gloriously analog in a digital world.

Glenn Close shows us how to build an outfit around a statement piece, in this case, a jacket from The Natural, the 1984 film in which she co-starred. Throw on navy slacks, loafers, and a crisp white Oxford shirt, and you’re good to go. Of course, it helps when you have iconic films attached to your name, too.

Example 1,088 of why denim-on-denim is always the answer to the in-flight outfit dilemma. Mr. Hoult opts for a charcoal-hued Canadian tuxedo, offset by black boots and a dad cap. Denim can take a beating. Whether from turbulence-induced coffee spills or an overenthusiastic recline, it provides a welcome layer of warmth on those cold and bone-dry flights.

As the oldest brother in Sweden’s Skarsgård acting dynasty, Alexander proves that an age-old graphic tee and Chuck Taylors will always be a can’t-miss combination. The louche, open trench coat adds a bit of flare to the fit. We also have to note, when you’re 6’4” with a chin chiseled enough to double as an ice luge, it’s hard for anything to look bad on you.

People love to claim that black and brown don’t belong together. I guess they’ve never had a Turtle Pecan Blizzard. The black shirt and blazer flirt with Y2K corporate-core, but the khaki-colored, pleated, baggy chinos and jazz shoes give the whole kit some much-needed attitude.

But for FW26, the spots are finally changing. While we’re absolutely not decreeing the demise of leopard (our love will never wane), there’s now a new pattern breathing fresh life into our autumnal wardrobes.

The easiest entry route may be a pair of calf-hair ballet flats or a working-week tote, but the most impactful approach? That has to be Mango’s stellar pair of balloon-leg jeans, which are destined to replace that leopard-print pair we know you were wearing all weekend long.

With a voluminous curved leg, this frankly excellent pair of statement jeans ticks off two major FW26 trends in one—and they’re incredibly flattering to boot (if you haven’t tried this silhouette yet, now’s the time). Priced at $90, they’re already selling out fast, so we suggest you move swiftly.

What to wear them with? Really, the options are plentiful. All the classics will work here: your white T-shirt, gray cardigan, cozy black sweater. Leather looks particularly chic—consider a funnel-neck jacket or slick black accessories. Sneakers and color-pop socks are your weekend go-to, of course. For smarter occasions, a dark taupe-brown lipstick will lend the look a little glamour, as will a pair of chunky silver earrings. And on your feet? Ballet flats now (a pointed style is an especially good move) and block-heel boots once the cold really sets in.

#6823. Skyler Gisondo on His New Fashion Campaign—and Dressing Like Harrison Ford in the ’90s

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The Primetime star is gearing up in Bonobos and getting ready for a very big 2027.

Skyler Gisondo is remarkably easy to talk to. If you’ve seen him on one of your various screens—whether as Decoy Dan from Primetime, Jimmy Olsen from Superman, or maybe just that meme of him from a decade-old red-carpet photo—you probably assumed as much. It’s the big smile, the friendly eyes, the freckles, the general sense of wholesomeness. But I can confirm it, because even though I know we’ve got a relatively brief window of time to discuss his new campaign with men’s fashion brand Bonobos over Zoom, we spend the first few minutes of our chat just … shooting the shit. It feels like catching up with a buddy you haven’t seen in a while. Relaxed. Natural.

Thankfully, the vibe continues as we start digging into matters of style. Gisondo tells me he’s always been interested in dressing well but hasn’t always known where to start. “I would see a cool dude walking down the street or something, and think, ‘Man, I want to look like that guy.’ But I never knew how. I always felt lost,” he says. He describes his 20s as a decade of “desperately trying on shoes that didn’t fit or something.”

He turned 30 recently, though, and “I really feel like over the last couple of years, I’ve homed in on my sense of style, what I feel good and confident in.” A very good time, then, to star in a fashion campaign—especially considering this seems like a breakout moment for the actor. He’s been working consistently since he was a kid, but his performance in Primetime as a young actor who gradually realizes just how toxic the entertainment industry can be has clearly launched him to another level. And he still has his upcoming role in Focker-in-Law this November and a couple more appearances as Jimmy Olsen (in Man of Tomorrow on the big screen and The People v. Gorilla Grodd on television) on the docket for 2027.

Over the course of our conversation, we touch on everything from dressing like a cowboy (a mistake) to using Harrison Ford in the ’90s as your style North Star (a very good idea). We also chat about the stuff he’s stolen from sets for his own wardrobe, the psychological validation of joining the Shrek franchise, and why, after Primetime, we can expect more creative big swings in the future. Read on for a few highlights.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

“It’s ultimately about your own confidence. I feel like the sweet spot for fashion is when what you look like reflects how you feel inside—when you get to this equilibrium and it allows you to be a more fully realized version of yourself. We all grow and our sense of fashion evolves with us but ultimately like I feel like there should be some current that runs through all of it. The stuff I’m drawn to is the more timeless, classic stuff. I look at Harrison Ford in the ’90s and I’m just like, it doesn’t get cooler, you know?”

“For a while, for whatever reason, me and every actor I know were like trying to look like a cowboy. And it just hit me one day: ‘None of us have ever worked a day in our lives on a cattle ranch, man.’ I don’t even know how to use a hammer! Like, what are we doing? Can we just be ourselves?”

“I’m pretty active. I surf and hike a lot when I’m at home. And I love walking; if I have an hour or two between meetings, I’ll just walk a few miles and take calls. I want something comfortable and functional, and I find a lot of vintage workwear just hits that and fits me well. And the story is so compelling to me. The idea of ‘Who’s worn this? What were they getting up to?’ ”

“What drew me to the campaign and to the clothes is that there’s a kind of timelessness to that style. My mom thought I looked amazing in the photos. My girlfriend too. My grandma and my sisters thought I looked great. It’s this very accessible and sort of classically cool thing they have going on. And I felt like me. I felt confident—so much so that I stole several items from the set.”

“With shows and movies, the fear is that it’s a one-of-one item that you might need back for another season. But that’s when you hit them with the ‘pretty, pretty please?’ You say, ‘I swear to God, I’ll guard it with my life.’ And they say, ‘Okay, but you can’t tell anybody.’ With a campaign, it’s probably easier because they’re excited for you to have it and represent. But probably 80 percent of my closet is basically just clothes stolen from characters and sets. It’s fun because you get to try on a bunch of versions of yourself and learn what you like.

“For instance, with Jimmy Olsen in the first Superman movie, they did a fantastic job with this retro-future thing. And then in The People v. Gorilla Grodd, they went a little more vintage-y in a way that felt more like me, Skyler, personally. I tried to steal almost the entire closet.”

“Well, right now I’m doing press for Primetime and Focker-in-Law. I’m doing another movie for A24 called Goblin that I’m not sure how much I can say about; I really don’t want to get fired. But I’m so excited. It’s the most insane script I think I have ever read, and it’s definitely a big swing. We have Man of Tomorrow coming out in the summer, and then Shrek 5. The number of texts I got when I got Shrek … ‘You made it, man! Oh my God! I had no idea you made it!’ I was like, ‘Thank you. Yeah, baby! Shrek 5!’

“But ultimately, it’s a very exciting moment because it’s the first time I have people asking, ‘What do you want to do?’ And I’m like, ‘Damn! I never really thought about that!’ I feel like Primetime lit a fire under me in a real way. And even though I’ve kind of been doing this my whole life, I feel a sense of drive that I’ve never felt really in this way before. So, yeah, man, I’m excited.”

#6821. The “Longevity Manicure” Is the New Quiet-Luxury Treatment That Will Save Your Nail Health

Why experts love this technique for your strongest, healthiest nails ever

Nail health has quickly become central to a professional manicure. Cumulative care, safe gel removal, and prioritizing long-term strength over quick aesthetic fixes are now standard, alongside high-shine, chip-free finishes. This new philosophy stems from restorative nail treatments taking over salons, from precision dry techniques like the Russian manicure to strengthening builder gels, likely driven by the wider beauty movement toward skin-barrier protection, regenerative treatments, and customized routines.

"The future of manicures isn’t just about the latest color trends or how long your gel polish lasts, but how well we care for the nails underneath," says Krisztina van der Boom, founder of DryBy. "The longevity manicure is the answer to that. It's about beautiful nails today, without compromising the nails you'll have tomorrow."

Rather than viewing nail care as temporary color, this manicure takes a skin-first approach, treating the nail plate and surrounding skin as just as important as the polish itself.

“Think skincare versus makeup; a traditional manicure is the makeup, the beautiful, glossy finish, while a longevity manicure is about everything underneath,” van der Boom explains. “It's all about looking after the natural nail."

Where a conventional gel appointment might focus more on buffing and thick gel overlays to mask imperfections, a longevity manicure uses tailored, restorative techniques. Examples include keratin treatments to rebuild weakened nails, LED red-light therapy to boost collagen and cellular renewal in the hands, integrating hand care into your routine, and microexfoliation techniques that clean the cuticle without damaging the surrounding delicate tissue.

To understand how a longevity manicure works, consider the full life cycle of a nail appointment. "We think of a manicure in four stages: preparation, application, maintenance, and removal," van der Boom says. "Traditionally, most of the attention goes into the first two—achieving that perfect, glossy, long-lasting finish. But what happens afterward matters just as much."

The core philosophy is to eliminate harsh mechanical buffing and aggressive chemical soak-offs. "Some of the most avoidable nail damage happens not when a manicure is applied, but in how it's worn and removed. That's why we place so much importance on thoughtful preparation, precision techniques, responsible maintenance, and gentle removal."

To do this, salons are drawing inspiration from advanced skin health technologies and incorporating high-tech tools and barrier-strengthening formulas into the treatment steps.

"It's about bringing the same thoughtful, preventative approach to our hands and nails that we've come to expect from facial skincare," notes van der Boom.

Whether your nails are naturally brittle, damaged from years of harsh gel removals, or simply need a healthier routine, this approach suits all nail types and needs. "The longevity manicure is designed as an ongoing ritual rather than a one-off treatment," van der Boom says. “With consistent, thoughtful care, the aim is to preserve the integrity of your natural nails, minimize avoidable damage, and support the skin of your hands over time.”

She believes this is all about prevention rather than correction. "You can disguise unhealthy nails with a beautiful finish, but there's nothing chicer than beautifully groomed, healthy nails even when they're completely bare."

Cuticle Hydration: Apply cuticle oil daily to support skin elasticity and keep the nail plate from drying out and becoming prone to chipping.

Protect the Skin Barrier: Treat your hands with the same care you give your face. Use moisture-rich hand creams formulated with ceramides or hyaluronic acid, and always apply broad-spectrum sunscreen to the backs of your hands to protect against UV damage and premature aging.

Change Your Removal Technique: Avoid peeling, scraping, or forcing off gel polish, which can strip keratin layers from the surface of your nail.

Try a Strengthening Treatment: Add repair treatments to your manicure routine, such as keratin strengtheners or at-home red-light therapy devices, for stronger, shinier nails.

#6818. Everything Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams Have Said About Their Friendship

HBO Max and Crave’s Heated Rivalry has quickly become one of the most-discussed series of the year, catapulting its stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams into the celebrity stratosphere. The two actors portray hockey players Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie), who have a secret love affair spanning almost a decade. The series is known for its spicy intimate scenes as well as its beautiful depiction of romantic yearning.

Storrie and Williams have been open in interviews about their experience creating the show, along with their offscreen relationship as they navigate sudden fame together.

“Hudson is my best friend, and I literally can’t fathom doing this without him,” Storrie told W magazine in December 2025. “We were both in similar places in life before this. We quit our jobs within a day of each other. We booked this and flew out the same day. Now it’s turning into two people who are being seen internationally for the first time. This has been the highlight of my life, and meeting Hudson makes that 10 times sweeter.”

Here, everything the two actors have shared about their friendship.

Fans of the show tend to “ship” Williams and Storrie, hoping they end up dating in real life. Storrie addressed this head-on in an interview with Vulture, saying things are strictly platonic.

When asked about the intimate scenes they shot in the show, Storrie said, “For me, it doesn’t feel spicy at all—like, that’s me and my best friend. This is the first time in my life I’m having this many eyes on me. They’ve seen me naked, they’ve seen me kiss, they’ve seen me be in love with a man on-screen—it’s only normal for people to try to transfer that over to mine and Hudson’s real life.” He explained that he intends to keep his private life private, adding, “I feel honored to be able to bring someone to life that so many people feel seen, understood, and represented by, and I think that transcends whoever I’m sleeping with in my real life.”

Williams expressed a similar sentiment to Deadline, saying, “I want queer people telling queer stories, but also, there’s the element of Connor and I—we’re best friends, and we love expressing that physically. You see people who infer or assume, and you kind of have to let that go. But then again, I never wanna stop expressing the love I have for Connor physically, and I’m never really going to, and I think multiple things can be true at once.”

In November 2026, Williams’s interview on The Assembly aired. One of the audience members there asked Williams if he ever had romantic feelings for Storrie. “No,” he replied. “Quickly, me and Connor realized we were, like, platonic soulmates, just completely in love with each other. I think that’s what made our friendship so stable and beautiful, is that we realized we could be completely ourselves, be completely guard down. So, I think the thing that made our relationship as rich as it was is, like, me and that man could cuddle for 10 hours, and it just mean cuddling, just mean we just love each other dearly, but don’t wanna beep each other’s bop.”

He then added playfully, “Who doesn’t want Connor Storrie in their shower? You know, someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day. I’m like, ‘Hey, I have a loofah but I can’t reach [my back].’ If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there.”

Sophie Nélisse, who plays Heated Rivalry’s Rose Landry, interviewed Williams for Wonderland magazine in January 2026 and asked him how he and Storrie balance promoting the show with forging their own identities. Williams admitted that they purposely go to different events, in part to keep their friendship more private and their brands separate.

“It’s been really nice, because Connor and I are aligned,” Williams began. “We want to be different artists. We don’t want to be the Olsen twins. We want to be Connor and Hudson, with different filmographies and different deals. As much as we love each other, our friendship doesn’t need to be public. Jacob [Tierney] has that quote: ‘Shane and Ilya are for the public. Connor and Hudson are for themselves.’ And that’s how we feel. People want to see us front row together all the time, but we actively avoid that, because it starts to feel like branding. If you’re always seen together, you become attached at the hip. I FaceTime him whenever I’m free. But if we’re offered the same fashion shows, we’re like, ‘Which one are you going to? Okay, I’ll go to a different one.’ We’re stubborn, selfish artists who want to be our own people. We’re like, ‘I love you. I don’t want to do everything with you.’”

Both Williams and Storrie got into great shape for the show. In a profile with GQ in December 2025, Williams talked about meeting his co-star and being intimidated by his build.

“Connor pushed himself up onto the island in the kitchen,” Williams said. “I remember seeing his arms. They were the size of my legs. I was like, Holy fuck.”

“It’s not true,” Storrie responded. “Because you have crazy legs.”

The show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, also commented on their affection for one another in the piece, saying, “They’re living through a thing right now that is bananas—absolutely fucking bananas—and they’re handling it with grace, with humor, with generosity. They adore each other, which is like, thank fucking God.”

While discussing his own workout routine with Men’s Health in January, Williams had a playful quip about Storrie’s physique: “I’m okay talking about my butt, but poor Connor Storrie—who has the fattest butt I’ve ever seen on a man—I’m sure just wants to stop talking about his beautiful cheeks.”

In a December interview with Entertainment Weekly, the friends discussed a viral video from the Heated Rivalry wrap party where they are rolling around on the floor together.

“Very plainly spoken, me and Hudson are freaks,” Storrie explained. “We’re clowns. We just love to riff and have fun and go crazy, and those were two situations where we were caught off guard doing our thing. The wrap party, that was all improvised. I think we were just putting on a show.”

Williams added, “Also, there might be something else, I think, with—we’re both very physical actors, and movement is a huge part of it.”

During his Vulture interview, Storrie spoke about moving into an apartment next to Williams’s while filming in Toronto.

“We would literally just go to set, go home, cook, work out together, and geek out over how excited we were to finally be working on this level,” he said. “If we were any less close, we probably would’ve gotten annoyed with each other really quick.”

The American actor told Vulture that they leaned into their chemistry while promoting Heated Rivalry’s first season. “If Hudson says something jokingly, like, ‘Spit in my mouth,’ I think that gives everyone else the go-ahead to get in on that too,” he said. “People are ruthless talking about our holes and our butts.”

During his discussion with Interview, Storrie added that spending time with Williams has helped ground them both during their press tour. “Hudson’s been in town, so we’ll have some quality time and come back down to ground zero,” he said. “It’s funny, because all the press and stuff is getting easier and easier and easier. You would think you would get burnt out and exhausted. Even though it’s only been three weeks of doing press for this, I’m clicking into an interesting sort of confidence and appreciation for all of this.”

Williams, meanwhile, credited Storrie for helping him keep the press tour fun during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “I have one of my best friends for life right beside me through it all, which is already a luxury that a lot of actors don’t get,” he said. “I’m sure I would’ve probably had a smaller appetite for the amount of stuff we’re doing if I didn’t have him through this. I’m an omnivert, leaning more to an extrovert, but I still get—I have ADHD, I’m unmedicated, currently, for the last while, so my social battery can just tap [out] pretty quick. At the end of the day, I’m pretty forgiving with myself if I’m talking with a reporter in a polite, more boring way. Then when I’ve had coffee, and I’ve had a nap, I let myself be chaotic. I let myself off the leash. I try to say, whatever mood I’m in, just be Canadian, don’t be mean. Whatever they get, they get.”

Timid magazine asked Williams how Storrie’s acting has helped him be a better performer. Williams responded, “He’s so incredibly present and so incredibly truthful. As an actor, it’s so much easier to think of what you should be doing or what you think would be an entertaining version of this or the most dramatic version or make sure you're hitting these lines properly or doing the scene properly or the director wants this and the script says this. But just to actually listen to the person and let what they’re saying affect you—Connor is so good at that. There’s so many moments where I am saying something and the script says he does this, and he does something so unexpectedly emotional or so unexpectedly vulnerable that even if I'm very robotic and going through a scene, he can crack me and change my trajectory in the scene. He’s a huge resource in affecting me and that makes my job way easier because I don’t have to. He makes me be present. He’s so good at that. That’s his superpower.”

Storrie, meanwhile, credited Williams for helping him understand Ilya so quickly in his Interview story. “I feel like I got the character pretty instantly,” he began. “I believed in his circumstances without almost any effort, and I just trusted Hudson so much. It’s so easy to act when you know where you’re coming from and you believe the person opposite you. I mean, I’m so gooey. I’m such a romantic. So any of the really heightened emotional moments—their love or confession or an outbreak or a fight—those are the moments that I really enjoy as an actor.”

Williams listed out all the nicknames he and Storrie have for each other during his Timid magazine interview. “He calls me Huddy, Papi, Bubba, Baby,” he said. “I call him Pookie. I used to call him Pookie a lot. Papi. Oh, Con Con. I call him that both in text form and verbally. But yeah, a lot of nicknames.”

GQ revealed that when the series wrapped, they got matching tattoos that read “SEX SELLS.”

The Canadian star revealed that he stayed at Storrie’s Los Angeles apartment when he came to the U.S. to do some press. “We were like, ‘Oh, my God, if people saw us just getting ready in the morning, giving each other big spooning hugs, just to say we’re proud of each other,’ people would be going crazy,” he told Variety. “If only one fan had access, God forbid. But yeah, we just love each other very dearly.”

The outlet asked him what creating Heated Rivalry taught him. Williams responded, “I think I had my own biases, maybe that would be too strong of a word, but my own discomfort if I expressed myself fully, physically and affectionately, both with women and men. It would feel inappropriate. I realized if you really do love someone—platonically or not—I’m such a tactile, sensory person. There are so many taboos. It’s much harder on men. I had to let that go, and I got to learn how freeing that is. That also went hand-in-hand with being myself, truly as an artist. Connor was also a great person to have at my side. I think we both opened each other up to just be freer, more fully expressive.”

During Williams’s January 2026 appearance on Andy Cohen Live, he revealed that Storrie is an “awful texter,” but they largely keep in touch with frequent video calls. “We'll Facetime each other or call each other randomly, very consistently,” he told the host. “That has sort of been my stability, especially through this. Just having my best friend who is in the same position I am.”

In a November 2025 interview with The Permanent Rain Press, Williams said he would pitch Storrie as “a beautiful little, sensitive little radical, artist boy. Who should be treated with the utmost care and hugs and friendliness because he can’t handle anything else. And that’s perfect. And that’s the way he should be treated.”

He added, “And anyone who doesn’t treat him that way should die.”

In May 2026, Williams and Storrie made their Met Gala debut. They took a bathroom selfie together, which Williams later posted to his Threads account.

The pair’s appearance at the Met Gala excited fans, with one user taking a solo shot of Williams and posting it alongside lyrics from Rihanna’s breakup song, “Woo.” (Williams has a longtime girlfriend, Katelyn Larson.) The post has since been taken down, but Williams responded and wrote, “Rpfing [real person fan fiction] gotta stop y’all.”

#6817. Our Last Chance to Save This Country Begins Today. Let’s Not Waste It.

Don’t even start thinking about the 2028 presidential election. Start thinking about what we’re going to do tomorrow and the day after that.

(Optional Video Accompaniment to This Post)

It is a decade now since the president came down the golden escalator and the country went straight to hell. All we’ve done as citizens of a self-governing democratic republic is squabble over the seating in the handbasket. Until Tuesday. Tuesday was nut-cutting time. Tuesday felt—probably rightly—like the beginning of an extended last chance that the country will have to spend every waking hour pursuing.

Just on Monday, the president closed out his demented road show with a weird address in front of one of his administration’s most conspicuous blunders: the Reflecting Pool. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court, with his carefully manufactured conservative majority, gave the boot to his latest attempt to ratfck the California elections, and the court did so without even a hint of an explanation. Then the president capped a rich, full day by bombing an Iranian island in the Persian Gulf, although I guess he went a little bananas on his little boutique website.

Mama said there’d be days like this. But she never said there’d be so many. And all the rest of them are on us. If I can offer one piece of advice it would be this: Ignore anything written that references the 2028 presidential election. If things break the way the polls say they will, there will be so much concentration required to do what we can to ameliorate the damage this administration has done and is capable of doing over the next two years. Starting the 2028 horse-race coverage this week would be yet another crime against poor, battered journalism. As the late Senator Edward Kennedy told a Democratic convention long ago:

Run through the tape, America. Finish the race.

#6816. All the Stars at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards

From Hailey Bieber to Elle Fanning to Pamela Anderson

Every fall, the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) brings together designers, editors, and the biggest names in entertainment to celebrate another year of American fashion. At a dinner held at New York City’s storied Natural History Museum, underneath a 94-foot-long model of a blue whale, new faces and tenured creatives alike are honored for their contributions to the industry—with awards such as the Emerging Designer of the Year and the American Accessory Designer of the Year handed out throughout the evening.

This year, the event was hosted by Keke Palmer, with presenters including the likes of Demi Moore, Naomi Osaka, Lupita Nyong’o, Matt Damon, and Cole Escola. Ralph Lauren took home the American Menswear Designer of the Year award (for the third time!), Rachel Scott of Diotima was awarded American Womenswear Designer of the Year (for the second time), and Ana Khouri was recognized with the aforementioned accessory designer accolade. Colleen Allen won the coveted Emerging Designer trophy, in a stacked lineup of nominees that included Lii’s Zane Li and Emily Dawn Long, among others.

In addition to the winners announced last night, several powerhouses were also spotlighted. Anthony Vaccarello, who recently announced his departure from Saint Laurent after a decade as creative director, was recognized as the International Designer of the Year, joined by YSL muses Hailey Bieber, Zoë Kravitz, Rosé, and Anja Rubik. Tory Burch received the Positive Change Award, Linda Fargo accepted the Founder’s Award in honor of Eleanor Lambert, and Gap Inc., under the direction of Zac Posen, took home the Innovation Award.

The Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award went to photographers Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin, Eva Chen accepted the Media Award in honor of Eugenia Sheppard, and the Isabel Toledo Board of Directors’ Tribute was awarded to Susan Cianciolo. Lastly, the Fashion Icon Award—previously presented to everyone from A$AP Rocky to Zendaya to Naomi Campbell—recognized architect Peter Marino.

Ahead, see all of the guests at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards.

#6814. The Best-Dressed Guest’s Guide to the Holiday Wedding Season

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Great dresses, fabulous accessories, and plenty of reasons to RSVP yes.

Gorgeous gowns, sleek stilettos, sparkling jewelry—there’s plenty to love about getting glammed up for a wedding. It’s a chance to have a little more fun with your fashion, whether that means wearing a more dramatic gown than you’d typically go for, trying a bold color rather than your usual neutrals, or finally breaking out those festive heels. Whether the invitation calls for a destination, beachfront ceremony or a cosmopolitan, black-tie celebration, there’s an art to dressing for the occasion while embracing your personal style.

And that’s why Bloomingdale’s is your go-to. From romantic florals and sweeping gowns to metallic heels, bold jewelry, and conversation-starting bags, there’s something for every kind of celebration. Ahead, 11 wedding guest finds so good you may even want to wear them for the holidays.

Moody florals feel especially right for a fall wedding, and Simkhai’s draped maxi matches the romance of a countryside estate or garden ceremony. This fluid, body-skimming silhouette is especially elegant; play up the deeper colors with burgundy heels and gold jewelry, or add a tailored blazer if there’s a chill in the air.

Make your bag the focal point with Cult Gaia’s sculptural olive-green clutch, complete with a wavy gold handle. The earthy color feels especially fitting for an outdoor wedding; pick up a floral-print dress in a similar shade, or pair it with butter yellow for a more unexpected color combination.

If there’s one shoe to have in your wedding-guest wardrobe, it’s a great gold sandal. Aqua’s strappy pair adds extra sparkle with crystal-trimmed buckles and a sculptural heel, making them a flawless match for everything from printed midis to black-tie gowns.

An asymmetric, off-the-shoulder neckline feels unexpected. The draped silhouette and uneven hem give it extra movement for a cocktail affair, especially when paired with sculptural earrings and barely-there heels.

A beach wedding calls for something a little more shell-ebratory. Simon Miller’s polished silver clutch has a playful seaside touch thanks to its sculptural shell shape and black tassel. It stands out against a silky slip dress or bold black gown.

Wedding guest dressing is the perfect excuse to bring out the statement earrings. Pair these BaubleBar chunky gold-and-blue studs with a simple one-shoulder dress for a minimalist cocktail look.

A black-tie invitation is your chance to fully send it, and this Amur gown delivers with dusty mauve silk, delicate lace appliqués, and romantic off-the-shoulder detailing. For an estate wedding or grand ballroom reception, add crystal earrings, a satin clutch, and a sleek updo to show off the neckline.

Loeffler Randall’s gathered leather design with gold ring detail keeps things understated but still has plenty of personality. Carry it with an evening gown or tailored suit for the big day, then bring it back out with jeans and a blazer for dinner.

A black-tie wedding invites a little sparkle. Jennifer Behr’s crystal-covered hoops bring the shine with a bold, rounded silhouette. Wear them with a strapless satin dress or a sharply tailored evening look, sweep your hair back, and skip the necklace to let the earrings catch everyone’s eye.

A printed floral slip dress is a stunning choice for a tropical destination wedding—especially one with an ocean view. Farm Rio’s fluid maxi looks beautiful with gold sandals and playful earrings.

Leave it to Jimmy Choo to make black heels feel anything but basic! With sheer floral lace, a pointed peep-toe, and a slender stiletto heel, these satin mules look especially gorgeous with a sleek column gown or silk midi for a formal evening wedding.

#6813. Duchess Meghan and Prince Harry Have Reportedly Moved Into a New Home

They have been living in the Cotswolds since late August, according to an insider source

A few months after Duchess Meghan and Prince Harry made their surprise move across the pond, it seems they’ve finally found a more permanent residence.

According to a new report from The Daily Mail, the pair have been living with their two children—Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5—in a friend’s house in the Cotswolds since they arrived to the United Kingdom in late August. The friend is allegedly a wealthy businessman who Harry became acquainted with through their mutual military charity work.

Originally, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were “living in the main house,” but now, they’ve “moved to a property on the estate,” per an insider source. Further details about the residence remain under wraps, though.

Meghan and Harry shocked the world when they revealed at the end of the summer that they would be returning to the U.K. for an extended period of time, six years after they stepped down from their senior positions as royals and moved their family to Montecito, California. (Currently, the pair are still holding on to their $14 million mansion in the starry West Coast neighborhood.)

The move precedes Harry’s 2027 Invictus Games, which are set to take place in Birmingham, England, and which may have partly inspired the move. Meanwhile, Meghan has already been busy at work too, teaming up with Malala Yousafzai for a project tied to International Day of the Girl, and joining Junior MasterChef Australia as a guest host.

In a recent interview with GQ, Harry opened up about why he and Meghan decided to move their family back to the U.K., saying: “Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn’t know how important it was to me.”

He added: “I think that having been [in the U.S.] for six years now and only being able to go back to the U.K. for short periods of time, to actually have my whole family there with me, the place that I grew up, wanting to be able to show my kids where I grew up and have them have the experiences to some extent that I had—the good rather than necessarily the bad—provided real, proper, serious thinking as to, ‘This is an opportunity, let’s do it now.’”

#6809. Pamela Anderson, 59, Pairs a Classic Red Manicure With a “Bombshell Bob”

The actress makes a case for minimal makeup and statement curls on the red carpet

In 2023, Pamela Anderson famously vowed to wear less makeup on red carpets. Since then, the actress has attended countless events makeup-free—but she has never left her hair behind. In fact, Anderson, known for her iconic long blond hair, makes her hairstyle the centerpiece, as she did last night at the 2026 Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) Fashion Awards.

Anderson walked the CFDA Fashion Awards red carpet in her typical minimalist makeup look, but with “bombshell curls” inspired by old Hollywood. In a black halter dress with feather detailing, accessorized with a just-bitten berry lip, Anderson wore a coiffed bob with old Hollywood pin curls. Because the curls fell away from her face, they showcased her glowing, fresh skin.

Anderson’s retro hair wasn’t the only statement look last night. She wore fall’s boldest nail trend—a bright, cherry-red almond manicure—contrasting with her satin black-and-white polka-dot clutch. With no shortage of buzzy new nail trends swirling around the internet, like “chili pepper nails” and “vanilla nails,” Anderson proves that sometimes the best shade for your manicure is classic red.

Lately, Anderson has given a master class in the many ways to style bobs. Just a few weeks ago, while at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles, Anderson wore a head full of curls with subtle bangs and lots of volume.

In an interview with Anderson last year, she shared her hair philosophy—why she never sticks to one style. “I think people associate me with big blond hair, but if I look at my whole life, I’ve always been one to change up the way that I look,” Anderson told Bazaar. “Your hair is another way to express yourself, and I’ve never been shy.”

She continued: “I guess I’m genetically blessed, but I’ve always had very thick, healthy hair. I do like to cut it and to style it differently. It’s freeing. I am a big lover of change; that’s what keeps us young and excited.”

#6808. Reggie Dinkins Is Still the Funniest Show on TV

Tracy Morgan and Daniel Radcliffe return for season 2 of their hilarious NBC sitcom somehow even wittier than before.

It’s a gross exaggeration to say that television is a lost art, but we can maybe agree that it has changed. Big-time. But sadly, not all of it is for the better. The binge model pigeonholes every show into a novel, scriptwriters tragically factor in second-screen doomscrolling, and the half-hour situational comedy has been driven to near extinction. Which is why I thank the television gods for The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins and then thank them again that it’s back so soon.

Still sharp, still absurd, and still just plain funny, The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins proves sophomores aren’t always in a slump, with a new season that picks up from season 1’s high point. “More of the same” isn’t bad news here, and if the series can keep pace, we might have a proper TV MVP when other sitcoms can’t make the cut.

Season 2 of Reggie Dinkins, which premiered November 2 on NBC, catches up with Daniel Radcliffe’s anguished auteur, Arthur Tobin, as he documents the show’s hero, Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan). Dinkins is a disgraced football superstar, and he’s hell-bent on rehabilitating his public profile. Arthur still lives in the Dinkins’ crowded New Jersey mansion that also houses Reggie’s levelheaded ex-wife and manager Monica (Erika Alexander), their son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), Reggie’s younger fiancée Brina (Precious Way), and Bobby Moynihan as Rusty, Reggie’s freeloading BFF who is too integral to the family’s cohesion to kick to the curb.

This season, Arthur grows ever closer to the Dinkins clan, despite his own hyperawareness of his documentary ethics violations. (Episode 2 of this season at last interrogates how compromised the in-progress project has been since the start.) Most of the ensemble, Radcliffe and Morgan included, exists in a sort of stasis—this is a network sitcom, after all—but it’s Precious Way who shines as the much-improved standout of the bunch.

Formerly “just” the younger woman in Reggie’s life last season, Brina has grown into the soul of the show. Along with Way’s buoyant charisma, there’s a newfound depth to Brina that wasn’t present in her before. I’ll admit, I thought she was grating at first blush, and I was ready to write her off as a shallow antagonist who didn’t seem involved with Reggie or the family in earnest. But in season 2, she’s evolved into a phenomenal supporting player who instantly brightens the room and contrasts beautifully with the others, most of all Radcliffe’s flummoxed British artiste. (A throwaway gag involving her “Voice Bucket Challenge” had me cracking up at my desk.) It’s a mere single component upgrade we’re talking about here, but it elevates Reggie Dinkins to a much higher degree this time around.

Jalyn Hall, too, grows in his once-thankless role as Reggie and Monica’s teenage son, Carmelo. Through a new overarching storyline involving a forbidden romance, which becomes a linchpin for most of season 2’s first half, Carmelo crystallizes in his specific variant of “Blerd” that is more refreshing than derivative. He’s not just “The Geek,” as you’d find in most sitcoms. He’s fluid enough to perform the function without killing the buzz.

The first four episodes of the season, provided to the press, keep up season 1’s winning formula—22-minute-sitcom hijinks that unfold against an airy atmosphere with well-timed punchlines. Daniel Radcliffe and Tracy Morgan further assert their powers as TV’s unlikeliest duo, and I can’t get enough of them. I pray there are yet more improbable excuses to ensure multiple seasons of a single documentary’s production. Sure, the rhythms are familiar now, but it’s welcome fun. Reggie Dinkins is a potent reminder of what television used to be and what it still can be if we’re brave enough to let it.

#6803. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6802. Jennifer Lopez’s ‘Frosted Pearl’ Nails Are This Season’s Dreamiest Manicure Trend: How to Try Them Now

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Between fashion week appearances and making a return to music, Jennifer Lopez has become a major beauty muse for fall 2026. The duo has added “frosted pearl” to the list.

In an Instagram post yesterday, Lopez sported a sheer base with a soft, luminous sheen; the result felt like a fresh take on classic chrome. According to pro nail artist Jessica White, the new trend features a reflective “glaze”—which Hailey Bieber famously popularized—but in a subtler way. “Rather than an intense, mirror-like chrome, it catches the light gently, giving the nails a pearlescent finish.”

Lopez’s natural blush-toned base color is essential to the frosted pearl effect, says White. “A sheer milky white or soft nude creates a delicate pearl effect, whereas a pinker base gives a warmer finish.”

With the colder seasons in full swing, understated, minimalist nail trends are to be expected; those who typically refrain from bold colors and elaborate nail art will often turn to traditional nudes, creamy neutrals, and your-nails-but-better manicures.

But White considers frosted pearl to be the best modern alternative. “There’s something about the subtle shimmer that feels a little more elevated and luxurious for the coming months,” she notes.

“For minimalists who want to introduce something a little different, it still feels clean, understated, and incredibly wearable, just with an added touch of luminosity.”

For the pearl finish, White explains that “chrome powder is the professional technique, but you can find chrome-like nail polishes, which are perfect for at-home.” Opt for one with a pink base. Sealing everything with a quality top coat will extend the life of your manicure and enhance the glossy shine.

#6800. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6797. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6796. A Look Inside the 2026 Dia Art Foundation Fall Gala

Attendees included Sofia Coppola, Marion Cotillard, and Matthieu Blazy

Last night marked a busy evening in the world of fashion. In New York City, the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards were hosted at the American Museum of Natural History, while in Los Angeles, a party was held to celebrate a new book documenting photographer Richard Avedon’s work in Harper’s Bazaar. But that wasn’t all—even more members of the fashion and art worlds united for the Dia Art Foundation’s annual fall gala in NYC.

The event acted as a celebration of two creatives—artist Roni Horn and British film director Steve McQueen—as well as a fundraiser for the arts. Guests gathered at the Dia Chelsea museum before migrating to a cocktail party and dinner where the honorees were toasted.

Some of the starry names in attendance included director Sofia Coppola and Oscar-winning actor Marion Cotillard. This is the first year that the gala has been sponsored by Chanel, after the French fashion house announced its partnership with the non-profit organization back in May. So, this naturally meant that Chanel’s current creative director, Matthieu Blazy, was also present (and he has been teaming up with the organization for years, even since he was at the helm of Bottega Veneta). In 2027, Chanel will sponsor the Dia Beacon gallery’s annual Spring Benefit luncheon, too.

Remarks were shared by the chairman of the Dia Foundation’s board of trustees, Nathalie de Gunzburg; the Dia director, Jessica Morgan; as well as by Matthew Barney, who paid tribute to Horn. Proceeds from the evening will go towards the foundation’s restoration projects, while also contributing to art-related lectures, commissions, educational programs, and more.

#6794. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6793. Louisa Jacobson’s Suited Streetwear Couldn’t Be More Different From Her Gilded Age Character’s Style

From corsets to bustles to floor-length skirts, the womenswear of the Gilded Age was known for many things. But Louisa Jacobson’s frayed raw hems and buckled collars were certainly not in the ladies’ 1880s style guides.

While doing press in New York City for the fourth season of her smash HBO historical drama The Gilded Age, Jacobson showed us a bit of her own street style... and it was a far cry from the looks that her character, Marian Brook, has donned on the very same streets.

Leaning instead into a bit of menswear, rather than the pastel gowns we’ve come to expect from her on-screen alter-ego, the actor experimented with suiting and modernized tailoring, thanks to the help of her stylist, Edward Bowleg III.

Last Monday, Jacobson turned to Mel Usine for a light-gray set from the label’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. Composed of a frayed, collarless jacket and matching inside-out skirt, the ensemble offered an unfinished, deconstructed look you’d have never seen during the 1883 Metropolitan Opera House opening.

It was layered over a black-trimmed white tank with a skinny red tie wrapped around her waist, and paired with peep-toe heels.

The next day, the actor pushed things even further, wearing a black-on-black monochrome look from Commission’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. This one was all about the buckle accents, with a zip-up blazer topped with a belted collar and little capri leggings trimmed with the same detail. In between was a pleated skirt, and for shoes, Jacobson wore pointed-toe pumps over calf-high socks.

Later in the day, Jacobson was a proper Calvin Klein girl—seen in Hudson Square wearing a dark-clay satin blazer and matching trousers with a heather-gray jacket over both. Her little nude ballet flats featured a contrasting reflective strap, and she grabbed a shoulder bag before heading out for an afternoon of press.

In an age of constant method dressing, it appears Jacobson is doing things her way.

With an eye toward the major races in Alaska, Michigan, Florida, Texas, and Maine, Karni laid out what the first 100 hours and beyond might look like for Hakeem Jeffries if Democrats take back the House. They also revisited Karni’s popular Vogue story from earlier this year, about compulsively telling everyone from Chuck Schumer to Steve Bannon about her divorce. As a reporter, Karni isn’t accustomed to writing about herself, so the experience gave her a greater appreciation for those who do. “I didn’t really mean to be brave, but a lot of people said I was brave,” she said, chuckling. “But mostly I was overwhelmed by people sharing their own stories. People clearly found it relatable.”

#6791. How to Choose a Graphic Print Bag That Won’t Go Out of Style

Exploring the power of pattern through the lens of Dior’s Cigale.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

A printed accessory can bring color, dimension, and personality to an outfit without requiring much else. The key is finding a design that works with the clothes you already own, suits your daily needs, and feels relevant beyond a single season. Dior offers an interesting case study, particularly when it comes to houndstooth, a motif closely associated with the house’s history and Christian Dior’s use of menswear-inspired fabrics in women’s fashion. The Dior Cigale bag, Mini Lady Dior Bag, and Bow bag give us a starting point for exploring the appeal of graphic prints and what makes a patterned accessory a worthwhile long-term purchase.

A graphic print should have enough character to stand out, but it should also work with the clothes you already wear. Houndstooth has a strong geometric pattern that can look just as good with denim as it does with formal, more tailored styles. If you prefer something more playful, a colorful or embellished design can make a familiar outfit feel different.

The bag’s shape and construction matter, too. Consider its size, how you plan to carry it, and whether the materials suit your lifestyle. A bag you intend to use regularly should be practical enough for your routine, with craftsmanship that holds up to frequent wear. The Cigale, for example, has a sculptural silhouette inspired by the architectural lines of a 1952 Christian Dior gown. That connection to couture gives the design a distinct identity, while its silhouette offers something to consider beyond the print alone.

A graphic print bag can work with a range of outfits, particularly when its colors complement the rest of your wardrobe. A black-and-white houndstooth pattern, for instance, pairs naturally with neutral knitwear and sharp separates. More colorful prints can coordinate just as well, provided you give them room to stand out.

The simplest approach is to keep the rest of your outfit relatively restrained. A printed bag can add interest to a white shirt and trousers or break up an all-black look without requiring a complete wardrobe overhaul. If you prefer a more coordinated outfit, pick up one of the bag’s colors in your shoes or another accessory. You don’t need to match everything. Just a little repetition is enough to make the look feel deliberate.

No accessory is immune to changing tastes, but some patterns have been around longer than others. Houndstooth, for one, predates Dior, but the designer incorporated it into his collections alongside other fabrics traditionally associated with menswear. He used these materials in women’s suits and dresses, pairing their masculine character with silhouettes that emphasized the female form. The brand continues to revisit houndstooth, including on the Cigale bag.

If you’re buying a graphic print bag to carry for years, think about whether you’ll wear it with more than one or two outfits. A pattern that works with your everyday wardrobe will get more use than one that calls for a specific look. It’s also worth considering whether you like the bag’s shape on its own. Trends come and go, but a bag you enjoy carrying for reasons beyond its print has a better chance of staying in rotation.

Start with the clothes you already wear. A graphic print bag can add interest to everyday staples like straight-leg jeans, a simple knit, and loafers, or bring some personality to office staples like tailored trousers and a crisp shirt. For dinner, try one with a black dress or a streamlined suit. The idea is to let the print add something to your outfit without making getting dressed more complicated.

You can mix prints, too. A fine stripe or small check can work with a bolder graphic, especially when the colors complement each other. If the combination feels too busy, simplify the rest of the look. With the Cigale, clean lines and structured tailoring can play off its sculptural shape. And remember, the bag doesn’t need much competition. A few well-chosen pieces will let it stand out without overwhelming the outfit.

A graphic print can draw you to a bag, but the details are what make it worth the investment. Look closely at the stitching, hardware, lining, and finish. The materials should feel appropriate for the price, and the construction should hold up to regular use. Consider how the print is worked into the design, too. The pattern should feel like part of the bag, not an afterthought.

With Dior, the appeal also lies in how the house approaches familiar motifs. Its graphic patterns are part of a broader design vocabulary, reinterpreted through changing silhouettes, materials, and embellishments. That gives the Cigale context beyond its appearance alone. Ultimately, a bag’s value comes down to what it offers in design and execution, not just the name on the label.

#6790. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6789. How to Style White Jeans for Fall

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

These outfits prove white denim has no off-season

White jeans are now a year-round staple, no longer relegated to the summer months between Memorial Day and Labor Day. From work-ready looks anchored by tailored denim to relaxed ensembles made for weekend getaways, these white-denim outfits do it all. This fall, take inspiration from a few of our favorite street-style looks. The lineup includes everything from straight-leg and relaxed fits to low-rise baggy silhouettes, in a range of soft hues like off-white and ecru. When paired with capsule wardrobe classics, such as a white T-shirt, a brightly colored button-down shirt, or a barn jacket, the results are stylish and equally easy to pull off.

Below, discover ten white jeans outfits that prove how cool they can look throughout the fall/winter months.

There’s a reason winter whites are a perennial favorite. Matching white jeans with your outerwear creates a clean, fresh monochromatic look. For a subtle sliver of color, layer an icy blue cardigan underneath, then add classic black pumps, and finish with sculptural gold earrings.

A simple way to wear white jeans during the fall is pairing them with a ladylike jacket in brown check print. The cropped silhouette offers a flattering counterpoint to relaxed denim, while black accessories—a roomy shoulder bag and ballet flats—lend a refined touch. Consider this an easy fall workwear formula you can wear on repeat.

If you’re a minimalist, try playing with contrasting textures to make your white jeans feel even more seasonally appropriate. Style them with a roomy black suede funnel-neck jacket, pointed-toe boots, and an unexpected accessory, like this elegant tassel bag.

The best fall outfits start with great basics: White straight-leg jeans, a white T-shirt, and a lightweight trench, which are all part of a well-rounded capsule wardrobe. Give these classics a hint of surprise by tying a pop of red knit around your shoulders and slipping into mules for an unexpected detail. They’re ideal for peak fall days, when it’s not too hot or too cold, and you can get away with a little peep-toe.

A striped long-sleeve T-shirt lends a touch of nautical charm to white jeans. Go for an oversized option in red to play up the relaxed, off-duty vibe. Black shoes—whether boots, loafers, or sleek sneakers—anchor the look, while a leather bucket bag and aviator frames complete the outfit.

Barn jackets remain a major trend for fall 2026. Make a case for wearing pastels well into the cooler months with a pale pink version and white jeans, offset by a black sweater, loafers, and a brown suede bag. Whether for a casual day spent running errands in the city or a weekend away, this combination strikes the perfect balance.

White jeans don’t always have to be worn in casual settings only. Make yours feel more elegant with a tuxedo-style blazer, silk camisole, and smoking slippers. A structured top-handle bag adds a polished finishing touch, taking the look effortlessly from desk to dinner.

Dip your toes into the season’s brightest color trends by putting a bright button-down shirt with otherwise simple styling pieces, such as a white T-shirt and straight-leg jeans. A leather belt and high-vamp shoes provide pared-back elegance.

French girls know how to layer the je ne sais quoi way, and denim is often the base. White jeans get a Parisian twist when paired with not one but three fall jackets—after all, temperatures are always unpredictable. A chore coat, plaid blazer, and windbreaker jacket can all be part of your layering essentials.

Nothing is more classically cool than wearing black and white during fall/winter. Bring your baggy white jeans into the winter months with a black turtleneck cardigan and sleek textural accessories—an embossed belt, suede flats, and a rich leather bag. Use this look as a base, then add a leather jacket or a tailored wool coat for extra warmth when needed.

Even if you had to stash this until spring, a knit polo like this for $41 is highway robbery—but luckily for any of you, it'll also crush under a blazer.

Before you balk at the linen of it all, notice the wool and also please know that linen actually holds its own in brisk temperatures and these will also crush in any temperature controlled setting.

This one is hardy enough for 9,000 foot peaks, so it will presumably be able to handle whatever you've got in store this winter.
